speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the federal government and the province of British Columbia have agreed to undertake jointly a low rental housing project in Vancouver, and a project for the development and servicing of residential land in Duncan, British Columbia, under the provisions of section 36 of the National Housing Act.
The housing project in Vancouver is being undertaken at the request of the city. It will consist of approximately 170 low rental units of various types, about 36 of which will be made available to senior citizens. This development is the second federal-provincial low rental housing project in the city. It is anticipated that it will cost about $1-| million. The project will be made available to families with low incomes. The rental should average about $44 or $45 a month. The cost of the project, as well as any operating losses, will be shared 75 per cent by the federal government and 25 per cent by the province, or by the province and the municipality if those two governmental bodies so wish.
This project will serve not only a very useful social need, but will provide as well additional employment opportunities to the construction industry in Vancouver. In the early days of the project it is likely that approximately 350 men will be employed on the site, and employment for a similar number will be provided in mills and plants off the site which manufacture housing equipment.
The project at Duncan, British Columbia, will also be undertaken by the federal-provincial partnership under section 36 of the National Housing Act, and will result in the development of an estimated 162 fully serviced residential lots for sale to prospective home owners. This project is designed to meet a growing shortage of serviced building lots in Duncan. It is estimated to cost approximately a quarter million dollars. As is usual in this type of project, the federal government will bear 75 per cent of the cost, with the remainder being borne by the province of British Columbia. When the services are installed these lots will be offered for sale at prices commensurate with the cost of development.
I wish to announce as well that the federal government has authorized the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make a grant of approximately $7,400 to the city of Trail, British Columbia, to assist it in carrying out an urban renewal study. This grant is being made under part V of the National Housing Act, 1954. It is hoped that the study will assist the city in identifying areas of blight and in developing an orderly program of redevelopment, rehabilitation and conservation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 14 the member for Winnipeg North Centre asked the following question:
Is the minister aware that the members of a Canadian Pacific switching crew in the Winnipeg area who felt that they could not cross a picket line two days ago have been informed by the Canadian Pacific Railway that their services are no longer required?
Will the minister look into this matter to see if there is not some protection for such employees under the national labour code, since these employees do come under federal labour jurisdiction?
Inquiries of the Ministry
My answer is as follows. I have looked into the situation, Mr. Speaker, and I am informed by the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that rather than being told that their services were no longer required, the employees in question were temporarily suspended pending investigation. Following the investigation they were returned to duty.
I am informed that disciplinary action was taken and I quote from the report I received:
Each crew member was returned to duty and assessed 15 demerit marks on the first offence and 25 demerit marks on the second offence.
I understand that such demerit marks are reduced by 20 for each subsequent year's clear service, free of discipline. Accumulation of 60 demerit marks is required for dismissal. At the moment all the men are back at work.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the first opportunity I have had to report to the

house with regard to the general trade situation of Canada, and to deal perhaps with other matters. The Department of Trade and Commerce ranges over a very wide field and it will be impossible, without taking too much time, to deal with all the aspects of such a large department. I should like at this stage to express my appreciation to the members of the department who have given me such expert assistance during the last several months. They constitute a very highly trained and competent section of the civil service.
I thought it might be wise to refer chiefly to two main matters; first the trade commissioner service, which is so widely spread throughout the world, and second, the general state of Canadian trade and development in relation to other countries.
The trade commissioner service is responsible for the promotion of Canadian export trade and for the protection of Canadian commercial interests abroad. Hon. members are, I think, well acquainted with the trade commissioner service and the very useful work the service has done in the past. Recently I had occasion to visit a number of our posts in Europe in connection with the sale of Canadian wheat and I must say that this very close contact with our trade commissioners in the field confirmed in my mind the high reputation which these men have acquired for themselves. It also confirmed the opinion which has been expressed to me on so many occasions by our producers, manufacturers and agriculturists that our trade commissioners are making a substantial contribution to Canada's well-being in the export field.
The trade commissioner service now has 57 posts abroad. These are located at strategic centres of trade throughout the world, wherever it is considered that possibilities exist for the further development of Canadian trade. The trade commissioners are constantly on the watch for opportunities to increase Canada's export trade and to safeguard Canadian interests abroad. From these posts reports are constantly received advising of foreign commercial policies and economic trends, on conditions in the territory, and at the same time bringing to the attention of Canadian producers specific opportunities for the development of trade.
While most areas of the world are covered by these 57 posts there are still certain sections which I believe warrant more intensive consideration. We have constantly under review the need for offices in these areas. During the past year, for example, 12 posts have been opened in Hamburg, Vienna, Colombo, Los Angeles, and just recently in
Supply-Trade and Commerce Accra. These new posts will aid considerably in the development of our markets in these countries. There are still, however, a number of areas where I believe we should have offices. The Middle East, in spite of troubled conditions, I think should receive better consideration than it is possible to give with our present offices. Consideration is being given also to new offices in the Far East, which is constantly growing more important to Canadian trade interests, as well as to establishing more offices in the United States.
The trade commissioner service at present comprises 127 offices. A high standard is maintained for entry into the service. Recruiting is by competitive examination held usually once during each year. Candidates must meet rigid standards as to education, physical fitness, age and general suitability, and they are drawn from all sections of Canada. Just last year 10 young men were accepted into the service. After a year's intensive training in Ottawa, during which time they are on probation, they are sent on a tour of Canada to acquaint them first hand with the Canada which they will represent commercially abroad. They are then posted abroad to work under the guidance of more experienced officers. Regular and annual recruiting into the service is essential if we are to maintain a young, virile corps of officers, and I hope nothing will be allowed to interfere with this.
I might add that from my own personal observations and meeting with these officers abroad, I have reason to believe that we are very well served in these stations. In addition to that, I have had quite a number of letters from businessmen who have been active in business interests abroad, reporting to me that they have been thoroughly served by our trade commissioners. I feel that our trade commissioners are a credit to Canada.
I thought I would continue, Mr. Chairman, with some remarks concerning Canada's present trade position. During the past year sales abroad have been subject to conflicting influences. On the one hand there have been extensive additions to capacity in the export industries, including a number of commodities relatively new in Canadian trade. On the other hand, there has been a general softening in world commodity markets and a decline in industrial output in the United States, particularly in durable goods. Renewed measures of restriction in the United Kingdom have been an important factor limiting further expansion in Canada's foreign sales, and in the case of wheat marketing difficulties have arisen from ample world supplies and have been accentuated by the surplus disposal measures of the United States.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
In these circumstances the value of Canadian exports for the first ten months of 1957 amounting to $4,026 million, on the basis of preliminary October figures, have been slightly above the corresponding period for the previous year. Items showing substantial gains compared with the previous year include uranium, crude petroleum, primary steel, iron ore, nickel, aluminum and flaxseed. The principal decline occurred in wheat and flour; in lumber, which was adversely affected by less residential construction in the United States and in the early part of the year by high ocean rates; in copper, which has declined substantially in price; and in aircraft following the completion of orders.
Looking at Canada's sales to individual countries, exports to the United States are up moderately while those to the United Kingdom have declined somewhat. There have been significant increases in sales to a number of European and Latin American countries and to Japan. The value of imports into Canada for the first ten months of 1957 amounted to $4,784 million, which remains virtually the same as in the corresponding months of 1956. Examination of the sources of these imports shows a decline in the value of purchases from the United States of more than $60 million or about 2 per cent, and an increase in purchases from the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries of $46 million, amounting in percentage terms to about 8 per cent.
With total exports up slightly and imports unchanged this year compared with last, Canada's merchandise deficit is slightly lower in the first ten months. In recent months exports have shown a firmer trend than have imports. Whereas in the early part of the year the deficit had increased compared with levels of a year ago, during the last six months it has declined. Continuation of this trend would bring a reduction in the over-all deficit in the period ahead.
Encouraging progress has thus been made toward two of the objectives of the present administration, the reduction of our large deficit on merchandise trade and the expansion of the share of our imports coming from the United Kingdom. We shall continue to pursue both these aims vigorously in the future.
I do not think any government in Canada's history has done so much in such a short time to implement its trade policies. Within a few days of assuming office the Prime Minister put before the prime ministers' conference in London a proposal for a commonwealth trade and economic conference. Then followed the meeting of commonwealth finance ministers at Mont Tremblant, where


there was unanimous agreement to hold such a conference next year. Indicating the importance we attach to our trade with the United States and other non-commonwealth countries, we met with Messrs. Dulles, Benson, Weeks and Anderson of the United States cabinet in Washington in October, and in the latter part of the same month I had the honour to represent the Canadian government at the ministerial meeting of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
We are hopeful that the commonwealth trade and economic conference next year will bring about a strengthening and broadening of our economic ties with the great family of nations to which we belong. It is not the intention of the government to interfere with the profitable trade we are carrying on with other countries. In fact we believe that the policies we are pursuing will put our relations with all trading partners on a healthier, more stable basis. In the last few years our trade with different countries has been developing in a lopsided and uneven manner. This may be good for some of the people some of the time, but it is bound to bring a reaction in the long run. An orderly and balanced growth of our trade will be beneficial to our entire economy. It will offer plenty of opportunities for other countries to do business with us.
I emphasized our interest in carrying on and increasing trade with all our trading partners when I attended the ministerial meeting of the general agreement on tariffs and trade at Geneva in October. Moreover, I assured the other members of GATT that this country would continue to operate its policies in accordance with the rules and procedures of GATT. At the same time I expressed the concern of Canadians that while Canada had, in the past, gone somewhat beyond its obligations, some of the other countries had followed policies which have had the effect of diverting a larger quantity of imports to our markets than would otherwise have been the case. Ministers were present at this meeting from many important countries, and I was most impressed by the constructive and co-operative spirit in which trade problems were discussed.
The most important matter considered at this session of the contracting parties to GATT was the European common market treaty. The members of this European treaty are at the same time important world traders and important members of GATT. It is essential to ensure that the European common market is developed in a way which will strengthen rather than weaken international trade relations. I expressed the views of

the Canadian government with respect to various aspects of the common market treaty which caused us some concern, and I indicated that the Canadian delegation would participate actively and sympathetically in the detailed consultations being initiated with the six countries concerned.
This session of GATT has already been concluded, and I am sure that the countries of the European common market are now fully aware of the difficulties which could arise through restrictive application of their treaty.
It has now been arranged that the GATT countries will pursue their consultations with respect to the common market-that refers to the common market treaty of next April- and I hope it will then be possible to obtain satisfactory assurances which will provide a basis of confidence and co-operation among all concerned.
I shall conclude my remarks at this time with a brief reference to the Canadian trade mission which is now in the United Kingdom. The reports that I received from that mission yesterday and this morning indicate that it is still having great success in its tour of the British Isles and has now been in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. The same enthusiasm on the part of British industrialists and British exporters is still being shown as it was a few days ago when I was there, and an increasing number of British business firms are asking for the opportunity of meeting with members of our trade mission in London next week. I reported when I came back from there a few days ago that 700 firms had asked to have the privilege of meeting face to face with members of our mission. That number has now gone up.
One or two questions have been asked with regard to what are the objectives of the mission. I set them out very clearly before the mission left this country, but it might be well to repeat that the purpose of the mission is twofold. In the first instance, members of the mission-widely drawn from all parts of Canada and representing at least 20 Canadian industries-are now in the British Isles looking at the state of British industry to discover whether or not that industry is in a position to supply the demands of the Canadian market in fields in which Canadian industry is not itself engaged.
The emphasis right from the very start has been in shifting to the United Kingdom some of the purchases that we now make elsewhere. There is no intention whatsoever of doing anything to interfere with Canadian industry. There is a very wide field for expansion of the United Kingdom market in this country, and there is also a very
Supply-Trade and Commerce wide field for the development of Canadian industry. When you consider that $5,700,000,000 worth of imports are brought into this country and that of that amount the United Kingdom enjoys only about 8J per cent or 9 per cent, you can readily see that there is ample opportunity for larger imports from the United Kingdom as well as for an expansion of Canadian industry so we shall no longer have to be too dependent on sources of supply in just one country.
The second purpose of the mission, which we have been stating over and over again in the United Kingdom, is to draw to the attention of the people of that country the advantages which we see here in Canada for trade on their part. We have pointed out to them that the Canadian people now number 17 million; that their per capita buying capacity compared with that of the people of the British Isles or other countries of Europe is equivalent to the buying power of 34 million people in those areas. In other words, our buying capacity per capita is double that of individuals in the United Kingdom and in Europe. We have also pointed out to them that our population is expanding and that as the years go by, and before the turn of the century, there is reason to believe that Canada will have a population of 40 million. We have also indicated to them that we have great natural resources which require development.
So we have set before the businessmen of the United Kingdom a picture of Canada providing a great expanding market. We have said to them whereas in the past your share of imports into Canada was 18 per cent and has now declined to 8J per cent or 9 per cent, we think you can regain your share of the market. We fully understand why you have had difficulties with the Canadian market; you made sacrifices in the war years in respect of your export trade, but now we see you have made a virtually complete recovery, and we are here to tell you that the Canadian market is available to you and we will assist you in any way possible in order that we may again create that triangular trade pattern which proved so beneficial to the United Kingdom, the United States and ourselves in the years prior to the war.
This is the purpose of the trade commission in England. It left here with the blessing of all parties in the House of Commons. The members of the mission are first class, representative Canadians, and they have entered upon their task with great seriousness. Many of them were a bit reluctant to travel abroad in the month of November with the prospect of returning just before Christmas, but when we suggested

Supply-Trade and Commerce to them that this was something they might do on behalf of Canada they responded with great eagerness. Furthermore, my observation of the members of the mission while I was with them was that they are as much interested and just as keen as any member of this house in stimulating trade between the United Kingdom and Canada and reestablishing that pattern of trade I have mentioned. Looking toward the future they see that as imports from the United Kingdom in Canada increase and the dollar earning capacity of the United Kingdom is correspondingly increased, Canada in its turn will benefit, because we have many things in this country which the United Kingdom used to take from us in the past and which we are ready to supply in the future.
The mission will be in the United Kingdom for another 10 days and will then return to this country. I hope that before we leave the United Kingdom arrangements will be made to continue the work of the mission in maintaining close relationships with the members of the government of the United Kingdom, the members of the dollar export council and other businessmen who are now showing so much interest in the work of this mission. I also hope that in the course of next year representatives of British industry will come to Canada to see for themselves what Canada has to offer to energetic and progressive men such as we have met in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
All told, I think Canada can be proud of the representative businessmen who are putting forward in the United Kingdom the situation as they see it and are doing their level best to encourage the expansion of trade between our two countries.

If, as I presume, by success he means the reception the delegation is getting from the United Kingdom, of that there can be no doubt; because the press gives us day to day reports on the tremendous reception the Canadian delegation is receiving.
But I should like to ask him what success, from a practical standpoint, the mission has accomplished thus far in the light of the two objectives he has just given. I should


like to know whether he would be good enough to tell the house what orders, either in number or in value, have been diverted from United States purchases to United Kingdom purchases along the lines, for instance, of those announced by the chairman of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario, who said he was purchasing $10 million worth of equipment? I thank the hon. member for Laurier for his comments. It is not possible at this stage to say that so many dollars' worth in orders have been placed in the United Kingdom, other than one or two which have already been announced. That news will come later. Some of the orders, of course, will not be placed this month. Business is not always done quite in that way. It depends on the type of material that is being supplied and the requirements of the country. If it is some project which is going to commence in Canada next spring, the order might be placed now or it might be deferred until January.
However, I say the mission has been a success for this reason. There was doubt in the minds of some people in Canada when the mission was proposed. There was doubt in the minds of some people in the United Kingdom when the mission was proposed. But over and above the kindly hospitality of the British people, which goes unquestioned and would be there for anyone who went over even on pleasure, the response has surpassed anything that was anticipated either on our part or on the part of those who have been responsible for the activities of the mission in the United Kingdom. The very fact that hundreds upon hundreds of British businessmen have asked to meet members of the mission surely indicates that there is a real interest in the United Kingdom in encouraging trade between our two countries.
It was not possible to estimate that interest before we left here or before the mission arrived in the United Kingdom. Quite frankly I may say that we anticipated a friendly response. You always get that in the United Kingdom. We anticipated a tour.

We have had an interesting expose by the minister of our position at the moment with respect to trade matters. I felt, however, that his remarks were more significant for what he refrained from telling the house than for some of the information that was provided. I think there is no dispute anywhere in the house about the admiration he expressed for the trade commissioner service that has been built up in this country. I believe all of us, particularly in recent years, have had tributes to that service indicated to us by businessmen with whom we were acquainted.
In the second place, the minister made reference to the position of exports and imports for the 10-month period of this year. I noticed particularly that he made the point that exports were slightly above those of last year. However, he is able to make an assertion of that kind only by merging the
Supply-Trade and Commerce trade record of the period of the year in which the former administration conducted the business of this country with that of his own. It just happens that by a fortunate coincidence the trade information for that 10-month period was made available only this morning in the press; and contrary to the trend and situation in the first six months of 1957, it shows that we have much to fear in the declines that are obvious in recent months under the administration of my hon. friend with respect to our export trade.
This report shows that for the month of October alone our exports to the United Kingdom have declined by $12 million as compared with the trade record of the same month a year ago, and indeed for the 10-month period are down some $55 million. Our trade with respect to the United States for the month of Ocober is also down to the extent of $27 million as compared with last year.

The Montreal Gazette has trade information this morning for the 10-month period. Furthermore, I do not think my hon. friend is at all justified in taking, as he did, full and complete credit for something in the nature of a change in the trend of the relationship between exports and imports. I find that the trend which he took some pride in describing this morning-that is, a narrowing of the gap between exports and imports-showed up in the first two months prior to the time when I think my hon. friend could take any credit whatsoever for guiding the trade policies of this country.
The figures for the period ending in July -and I am sure my hon. friend would not think he had any influence on trade at least up to that time-indicated that our exports were not going down, as I have indicated they are now going down to our principal markets, but they in fact showed a very advantageous increase. In the two previous months described at the end of July there was a narrowing of the gap between exports and imports because imports were on the decline and exports had continued to rise.
It is perhaps trite to say that Canada lives by trade, but probably that is truer with respect to Canada than with respect to any other country in the world, because Canada's population is not large in relation to the huge international trade volume which we have in this country. I think all hon. members of this committee know from the experience of the depression years just how long it takes

Supply-Trade and Commerce to recover from the effects of bad trade policies. Consequently I believe there will be considerable alarm and anxiety when we find that in recent months our export trade is showing a decline such as was indicated in October and in the examples I gave a few moments ago.
A great number of Canadians, a majority of them perhaps, depend directly or indirectly on export trade. We require exports for at least two-thirds of our normal wheat production. We depend on exports for 95 per cent of our paper production and perhaps about 80 per cent of our aluminum production, to make reference to just some of our notable exports. These are, of course, important items of external trade; but in addition to that Canadians are very concerned with elements of internal trade. While I have indicated that there is a very alarming drop in our exports in international trade, many Canadians are similarly alarmed these days about some very unpleasant differences between trade statistics and business statistics of the present time in relation to the period when the former administration left office.
I could give just a few illustrations. In June the index for stock market industrials was 303. In October, according to the Bank of Canada report, copies of which we all received the other day, that was down to 228. The wholesale price index with respect to grains in June was 171.9. It is now 168.7. The livestock index wholesale in June was 292.9 and is now 285.7. We have already had several indications of what happens when trade volume declines, and we know that the employment picture, the number of persons seeking work and who are without jobs, is also extremely alarming when one compares June with the current situation.
In respect to new orders, also an item dealt with in the Bank of Canada report to which I referred, I find that in the last available period, September of this year, new orders received amounted to $1,692 million as compared with $1,812 million a year ago, and that compares with the June figure of $1,754 million. If one goes to another important aspect of domestic trade-and I refer to the volume of industrial production-one finds that in June when this administration left office the index figure, which is also shown in the Bank of Canada report, was 296.9 and in August it had declined to 286.5. The manufacturing index in June was 296.2 and in August the last available figure showed that there had been a decline to 283.1.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it one o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, in resuming the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce after the noon adjournment I simply want to say my recollection is that on general statistical information he suggested that never before had the policies of a new government made themselves evident so quickly. Well, in that respect I think I will agree with him. I want to continue with some of the statistics that I was referring to prior to our noontime adjournment. However, these statistics are, I think, ominous.
During the recess I inquired, and I found that on June 1, 1957, the average weekly wage of labour in this country in manufacturing was $65.08. On September 1, which is the latest available statistic, it was $64.60. There is thus a decline and that decline is not normally to be found from June to September. In addition, when we are speaking, as we are in committee, on trade, I cannot think of anything that is more related to the volume of trade than perhaps the figures on railway carloadings. On November 21, 1957, car-loadings were 769,926. A year ago they were 837,749.
Another item that I think is very significant when we speak of trade is the average hours worked per week by our labour force. This is something that had been rising steadily prior to the advent of this administration. On September 1, 1957, the average hours worked per week were 40.5; a year ago they were 41.1. I think most hon. members will agree with me that this figure is significant. I find it so in my own riding. While as yet we have not in Kenora-Rainy River people wholly unemployed in a significant way, perhaps I do find that the take-home pay in the work week is very much reduced from what our workers had experienced previously, and that is one of the ominous features to which I have referred.
In his remarks the minister referred again to the United Kingdom trade mission. I did feel when he introduced the subject on Tuesday that anticipating these estimates, he could very well have made his remarks at this time; but, unlike his predecessors who also have some travelogues to disclose, he chose that particular time to deliver his remarks. I recall that the leader of this group was very gracious, as I think I attempted to be, in a personal phone call to the minister to wish him well on this mission, and I do not propose to quarrel in any respect with the objectives of the mission. My quarrel is simply with the double talk and with what I call the

politics which are being played by the minister with respect to this particular mission.
When I refer to double talk I will give illustrations, but I think hon. members will recall a former correspondent in the press gallery who was one of the severest critics of the previous Liberal administration. He was the correspondent of the Toronto Globe and Mail, George Bain, and is now a resident correspondent in the United Kingdom. On the very day the minister was reporting to this house about the activities of this mission, Mr. Bain had this to say with respect to the tour of this Canadian mission in a dispatch to the Toronto Globe and Mail, which is unusually friendly to the Conservative party: This has been a busy week for the platitude.
If the new trade resulting from the visit of this mission ever reaches the volume of the cliches which have been expended in pursuit of it, there will need to be traffic lights installed in midAtlantic to regulate the traffic.
Another point in connection with the mission-I am not dwelling too much upon it- is simply this. I felt the minister was very evasive this week since his return from the United Kingdom on questions raised by the hon. member for Essex West, the hon. member for Coast-Capilano and the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet and others on the types of factories that were visited by this mission. The minister was present in the United Kingdom until the end of last week. He himself, in his statements to this house, has indicated that the first portion at least of the visits arranged to these British factories was arranged by what he described as an official committee, I think a committee acting under the direction of our high commissioner to the United Kingdom, Mr. George Drew. I feel that before we leave these estimates the minister should name the factories and the types of business done in those factories that the visit was officially arranged for by this committee.
I noted with some regret in the minister's remarks on Tuesday that in reference to the portion of the delegation that represented agriculture in this country they seemingly were directed in their travel tour in Britain to visits to their trade and occupation counterparts. Now, this I think is rather a surprise. I believe certainly the agricultural representatives in the house would have expected that their tour would have been directed more to possible purchasers of the products of their trade. Anyway, this has been certainly a very unusual trade mission because, unlike any other trade mission I have ever heard of previously, it seemed to have no thought of sales in mind.
I spoke of double talk, and I am going to give some illustrations to explain why I used
Supply-Trade and Commerce that term. I think it was the Toronto Star which said that in all attitudes toward United Kingdom trade the present administration seems to have-and I quote-"a miracle of exquisite timing". Hon. members will recall that just prior to the arrival of the United Kingdom delegation in September, invited here to discuss expansion of trade, the Minister of Finance referred the textile trade to the tariff board anew.
Another illustration of the double talk of which I accuse the present administration is the fact that while they are flying the flag of British trade, so to speak, most of us know that at this very moment there are representatives of the government at Geneva discussing trade with the governments associated in GATT. Those delegates of Canada are asking for increased tariffs on such things of importance to the United Kingdom as iron and steel, in which the volume of trade amounted to $50 million last year, and pipes and tubes, in which the volume of trade was some $17 million. When we discuss this question of flag waving and sentiment with respect to trade, I simply want to say that I do not think anybody would accuse the former shrewd minister of trade and commerce of anything along these lines.
On the other hand, let us look at the record of trade between this country and the United Kingdom under his regime. In 1955 we bought British-that is what hon. members opposite are always preaching, buy British- to the extent of $401 million of goods from the United Kingdom. In 1956 that figure rose to $485 million. In the first half of 1957, with which the former administration was associated, purchases amounted to $260 million. I think that without talk and without flag waving there has been a very keen recognition of the value of this type of trade, and I question whether that is continuing in any substantial way today so far as actual dollars and cents are concerned.
A conference was held at Mont Tremblant early this fall. I know some of the consequences of that conference were rather shaking and shocking to my hon. friends opposite. I believe they came to learn that there was somewhat of a difference between rhetoric and reality. In any event, I feel that the House of Commons, discussing now the trade estimates of the new government, is entitled to information that so far has been hidden from parliament with respect to the pros and cons of the proposition presented by the British delegation at Mont Tremblant. Surely the minister will be able to tell the committee as we discuss this problem just what the proposition is all about, what the merits are and what the demerits might be.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I think the people of the country generally felt very disappointed with the new administration in this respect. This conference took place some time after they assumed office. I do not think there is any member of the house who will not agree that the Financial Post is most impartial in its criticism either of the former administration or of the present administration, but this paper had the opportunity to do something that we in the opposition have not had the opportunity to do. This paper, the chief paper in the country of this type, had a very competent observer at the conference, and on October 11 the Financial Post had this to say with respect to the Canadian representation at this very important conference:
The unfortunate fact is that the Mont Tremblant conference between Canadian and British officials was a great flop. The whole story of what went on behind the scenes is now available. The British had prepared very thoroughly for the meeting. The Canadians had not.
I think we should expect the minister to make some answer to this indictment. I wish to refer to another publication which I think we also recognize as not being local in distribution, and which has a very experienced parliamentary correspondent. I refer to Macleans magazine. Blair Fraser refers to questions very properly asked the Minister of Finance by the representatives of the press following an outline of the trade proposals at the Mont Tremblant conference from the British delegates, proposals which had very substantial possibilities. Blair Fraser asserted that the Minister of Finance had been everything but frank with the journalists of the country when interviewed with respect to the implications of the British proposal, and went on to say:
None of his stone-walling did much good. Rightly or wrongly, everybody in the room-
He had reference to the large delegation of representatives of the press.
-was convinced that the reason he couldn't talk about Canada's proposals was that Canada had no proposals worth talking about.
Basically discussion of trade at the moment has a relation to diversion of imports from the United States to imports from the United Kingdom. During the present session there have already been very worth-while comments from this side of the house with respect to this possibility. I recall that the hon. member for Algoma East made a very important speech. Mr. Clark Davey, a press observer who is not noted for favouring Liberal assertions made in parliament, had this to say about the speech of the hon. member for Algoma East: "A devastating attack on Conservative trade policies." With


respect to diversion I am in complete agreement with the hon. member for Algoma East when he said:
I am not so much Interested in diversion of trade as I am in building up and increasing trade.
I think that is something that would be supported generally by the members of the party to which I belong. With respect to the matter of double talk, I also point to the strong evidence that the administration has been talking not bilingually but certainly in double talk when it has talked differently to London and to Washington with respect to its intentions in the matter of the diversion of 15 per cent of our purchases from the United States. There is every indication that when they went to Washington they said to the officials there in a very pious manner, ''Oh, dismiss this; this is long term, nothing immediate, not something about which you should get very excited."
That brings me, of course, to the very important discussions that did take place in Washington. A major portion of our trade is with our immediate neighbour. The conduct of Canadian relations with the United States is probably the greatest problem that faces any Canadian administration. It faced the former one. United States relations dominate all economic policy and vitally affect all business, trade and finance in this country to a very important degree.
Again, I think the results of that visit by the four cabinet ministers of the new administration were much less than would have been expected, having regard to the tough talk that we all remember from them during the election campaign. I think the very high expectations are certainly mocked by the very small achievement. In this respect again I cannot, from any personal observations, make any comments as to the result outside the communique that is normally provided after these conferences. But others who were there and who are independent, certainly politically, have made some comments. I do not choose to quote anyone who is known to be unduly critical of my Conservative friends who are sitting opposite to us at this moment. I refer now to Mr. Arthur Blakely, who I think is probably among the foremost noted journalistic critics of the former Liberal administration. With respect to this conference in Washington Mr. Blakely, writing in the Montreal Gazette of October 11, had this to say:
The four Canadian cabinet ministers who went to Washington earlier this week to negotiate with Uncle Sam for the settlement of some mutual economic problems, came back empty handed.
Then he went on to say:
There have been other pilgrimages to Washington which could be said to have produced nothing.

But it's doubtful if there have been any which could be said to have produced less than this one.

I thank the committee. I should like to refer to another report from a Canadian journalist following this Washington conference. I refer to Mr. Ed. Hadley, whom I had the pleasure of meeting myself when I was in a role somewhat similar to that of this delegation when I visited the United States a year previously. There will be no change in United States wheat disposal methods beyond that which halted barter deals last summer.

Mr. Hadley goes on to say:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker's suggestion for a 15 per cent switch of Canadian foreign purchasing from the United States to the United Kingdom was "played down" at the meeting here.
I must conclude my remarks, because I know there will be a further opportunity to speak on the individual items. I simply want to say to the minister, as I said in the beginning, that I felt there was much lacking in the information he gave us in his opening remarks. His department, as he said, is a most important one. It has been led in the past by Mr. Howe, a very distinguished Canadian whose achievements probably make it somewhat difficult for the new minister, but I am sure the new minister will apply to the department also conscientious activity.
I am sure the committee will expect to hear from him, while these estimates are before us, something about the policies of the administration with respect to uranium and
Supply-Trade and Commerce atomic energy, something that I had hoped to deal with in some detail but time has not permitted; and the gas and oil export policy of the government, particularly with respect to possible approval of new pipe lines. I think all of us are very concerned today about any governmental support that might be given to research programs, particularly the sponsorship of students in scientific fields. I feel, too, we shall have to pursue a little beyond the remarks of the minister the references to the European free trade area, particularly now that Great Britain has indicated a likelihood of joining it. I believe there has been some change of attitude in relation to Canada's contribution to the Colombo plan. I should like to see a further review of that.
Perhaps the minister at this time could give us, even on an interim basis, some indication of the public and private investment to which we might look forward in 1958. I realize that this is normally the subject of a white paper that is produced in parliament in July and February of each year, but I am sure his very able staff has already given the future some review. I thought perhaps even an off the cuff prediction relating to this very important matter might come from the minister. I thank the committee for giving me some extra time for these comments respecting trade and commerce.

It struck me that the minister had left out a great deal. I am not saying that as any particular criticism, because we all know that this is the first occasion on which the minister has presented his estimates. But it does seem strange that the minister, in introducing the department, seemed to leave out completely one very important wing of his department. That is, he made no reference whatever that I could detect to the agricultural side of his department. It could be said that in the main, matters dealing with agriculture would come

Supply-Trade and Commerce under the Minister of Agriculture. However, when it comes to the wheat board, the marketing of grain, the setting of grain prices, those things come under the jurisdiction of this minister.
I was disappointed that at a time like this, when even members on the government side have recently expressed concern over the continuing crisis in agriculture, the minister had not one word to say as to the government's policy with regard to the wheat board, marketing, agricultural surpluses, or any of these allied subjects.
I will have occasion to refer to that a little later, but first I want to make a comment or two on what the minister did say.
He started off by talking about, and in fact he took some pride in, what this government had done. I am not using his exact words, but the import is the same. He said they had done more in a short time than had been done by any other government in the way of implementing trade policy. Certainly I do not wish to take away from the minister any of his success, but when he speaks about the trade policy of this government I respectfully submit that he is talking about something which has not yet been announced. What is the government's trade policy?
We on this side of the house have been patiently waiting until the opening of this department's estimates in the hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would get up and state what the government's trading policy actually is. He failed to do so, but instead told us that he takes credit for having implemented such a trade policy. I hope before this debate ends the minister will take care of that great omission and let this house know what is the trade policy, because at the present time there is a grave doubt in this house and in the country as to the existence of such a thing.
I am saying this out of kindness to the minister. As a colleague from Manitoba I am really concerned about his future in the government-

*-because there is a trend going on which I think holds certain dangers for the minister. In the past his predecessor in office was referred to as the minister of everything, perhaps with some justification, because he had the Department of Defence Production to look after and he had charge of a great many branches and divisions of the government, but I notice that in the new set-up defence production has been handed over to the Minister of Public Works, and the setting of whatever has been set

about trade policy so far has been done by the Minister of Finance. The conference at Mont Tremblant was left to his tender care and was handled with what can only be described as disastrous dexterity, and I am afraid that little by little the Minister of Trade and Commerce will find that his powers and responsibilities are going to be chipped away until he finds he is not going to be the minister of anything.
For this reason I think it would be very desirable for him to discover, first of all, what is the trade policy of his government, if such a thing exists, and to relate this policy to this house and then do his best to bring it into effect.
The minister made reference to the commonwealth conference which is to be held. Well, of course, we cannot debate something which has not taken place, but there has been a preview of what might take place at that conference in the Mont Tremblant conference; and there, as was pointed out by the hon. member who spoke before me, an offer was made by the government of Great Britain, through its representative, and the Canadian government absolutely ignored that offer. In fact the Minister of Finance did worse than that; he threw cold water on it before it had even been properly examined.
I know we may have differences of opinion, perhaps mainly in degree, as to what could be done and how quickly it could be done with regard to the establishment of a free trade area as between the United Kingdom and Canada, and I realize there are many considerations which must be taken into account. However, prior to June 10 the members who support the present government and the ministers of that government were most vocal across the country, and even on many occasions in this house, about the desirability-in fact almost the desperate desirability-of negotiations and trade with the United Kingdom. They had some pretty strong words to say on occasion, although I will not take the time of the committee to repeat them now since they are all on the record and easily found.
However, the impression was left in the country that the present Prime Minister, as soon as possible after the election and provided he was then Prime Minister, was going to make some sensational offer in order to increase trade between the United Kingdom and Canada. Well, the election came and went and the government sat tight, made no offer whatsoever. Then the government of the United Kingdom made its offer, which I still believe was a very statesmanlike one in all the circumstances. Instead of acting on it, instead of even giving some lead

on the principle of that proposal, the government immediately started to scurry for their foxholes. Not only did they scurry for their foxholes, but they pulled the holes in after them. Since then there has been a sort of iron curtain drawn around the whole question with, once in a while, the Minister of Finance coming out with some statement or other, but no clear-cut policy and no statement of principle on this question from the Prime Minister or anyone else.
Here I thought there would be a grand opportunity-and I was sitting here in eager anticipation-for the Minister of Trade and Commerce, having just returned from Great Britain where apparently he was very well received and where he said the response to the trade mission was just out of this world, to rise in his place and place before this house the attitude of the government toward the offer. Instead of that we have a travelogue of what this trade mission was supposed to be doing in Great Britain, so I suppose we will have to confine our remarks to that phase of the matter.
What has he told us about the details of the trade mission to the United Kingdom? He has told us the mission had a twofold purpose; first, they were supposed to check on the supply or potential supply of goods which could be produced; second-and I want the hon. members of this house to mark these words, as they are of great interest-to draw attention to the possibility of trading with Canada. Now, when you compare those words with some of the thunderous phrases heard in this house and throughout this country as to how we were letting down the United Kingdom and how there was almost a question of refusing to trade with that nation, it does seem a little strange. Here we have the minister coming directly from the United Kingdom and saying that one of the purposes of the mission was to draw attention to the possibility of trade with Canada. That, Mr. Chairman, is the understatement of the year.
If all that mission was supposed to do was just draw attention to this possibility, then I respectfully submit that we could have saved a great deal of money and trouble by having the Prime Minister write a letter to the chancellor of the exchequer or the Prime Minister of Great Britain in which he could have drawn attention to it.
I believe there is a very serious omission in this whole business. The minister has repeatedly stated that the chief purpose of the mission was to arrange for purchases by Canada from the United Kingdom. Well, I have no objection to that; I would like to see a great many such purchases made, but
Supply-Trade and Commerce surely the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not head this delagation simply as a sort of glorified purchasing agent for Canadian business. Surely he must have had in mind, or the government must have had in mind, that his was a department of trade and commerce, not just commerce. He must have forgotten the trade part of it. The people who are primary producers in this country, such as those engaged in agriculture, wood products, base metals and many others, certainly expected the Minister of Trade and Commerce to have made at the same time some arrangements for the export of Canadian primary products to Great Britain.
As a matter of fact when he made his report we addressed specific questions to the minister on what was being done in that field and what discussions were held by the members of the trade mission, government officials or the minister himself with respect to increasing the flow of Canadian primary products to Great Britain. His answer in every case was that the chief purpose of the mission was not to sell but to buy. Well, now, I do not think that is good enough. We have a minister and a Department of Trade and Commerce, and we expect some trade and not just commerce.
We expected that the minister should have been a trader and should have taken advantage of his visit to the United Kingdom to enter into negotiations, to have initiated at least preliminary talks about trade agreements that could be entered into-long-term bulk trade agreements-in order to assist the export of primary products from this country, which is one of the essentials in our trade picture.
Then the minister also stated-and that was the only part of his report that I thought contained any reference at all to government policy-that it was the policy of the government that they would not interfere with the trade between Canada and any other country. Of course at that point the minister was really humourous, and I am glad it was he who said that rather than the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, being a westerner, at least has a sense of humour; and certainly he must have seen the humour in that statement. When he states that it is the policy of this government, or of any Conservative government for that matter, not to interfere in trade between Canada and any other country, he is stating something that is obviously funny.
When one looks at our tariff structure; when one looks at the elaborate tariff structure that has been built up over the years, chiefly by Conservative administrations, one

Supply-Trade and Commerce certainly can see that is not a policy of noninterference. Every day this government, through its actions and its tariff policy, is seriously and substantially interfering with trade between Canada and all other countries, even with respect to the United Kingdom.
That again points up the humour of the situation, or the irony of it. We send a trade mission over to Great Britain ostensibly to increase purchases in that country for export to Canada; and while the Minister of Trade and Commerce is over there promoting that phase of it, the Minister of Finance here at home is busy trying to find ways and means of preventing imports from Great Britain by making, very obviously, plans to increase tariffs against British-made goods.
Look at our tariff structure today. Are we, on the one hand, going to ask the manufacturers of Britain to send certain articles for sale here in Canada, and at the same time point out that we have a duty of 20 per cent or 25 per cent against those goods? When we are saying to them, "We want to trade with you", on the other hand the Minister of Finance is saying to them, "We are trying our best to keep your products out of Canada". That is supposed to be a policy of non-interference with trade. That is supposed to be the policy of the present administration.
I have quoted figures previously and I want to remind the house of them again. In the last 10-year period alone the consumers of Canada have paid in duties on imports coming into this country from all countries in the world just about $4 billion. That is supposed to be a policy of non-interference on the part of the government.
I believe there is a policy they could follow. I believe the policy of this parliament should be designed to remove, so far as it is possible and practical, the trade barriers between this country and the United Kingdom in the first instance; and having accomplished that, we should continue to do so with all commonwealth countries and with as many other countries in the world as we can.
In other words, as an expanding country engaged in primary production to the extent that we are engaged in it, and that being the basis and foundation of the wealth of this country, I believe our whole policy should be aimed at the removal of trade barriers. But I am very much afraid that the policy of the present government is the very opposite. Their whole proposition of, on the one hand, pretending to be expanding trade with the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries and on the other hand of doing their best to prevent that trade through

the tariff structure, is one that I think they are going to find will lead to disaster.
It is still fresh in the memories of the Canadian people that the period from 1930 to 1935, when we had the second last Conservative regime in Canada, was the time when we had possibly the highest tariff srtructure in the history of this country and was also the time when we had the greatest number of unemployed, the most disastrous farm prices, and the greatest depression. I am not going to lay at the doorstep of the tariff policy the whole depression, but certainly the two were very closely related.
There are those who sometimes repeat slogans rather than express opinions and who say, "We must see to it that other countries do not export their unemployment to Canada; we must have protection". We must examine slogans of that kind very carefully, because we must always remember that for every dollar's worth of imports that come into this country, eventually we can pay for it only by a dollar's worth of exports. To the extent that we are going to pay for our imports with exports, that in itself is providing employment. Certainly the last flirtation we had with high tariffs in this country in 1930 to 1935 taught us the lesson that you cannot prevent unemployment by raising your tariff structure.
What the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River pointed out in his speech-and I agree with him heartily-is that we sometimes forget about the internal trade of our country. If you will look at the figures and will look over our economic history for the last 30 or 40 years, I believe you will find that the level of employment or the level of prosperity in this country has been directly related to our internal trade. I am not discounting at all the importance of our external trade, but the level of internal activity as between Canadian and Canadian is still the basis and foundation of our full employment in this country.
I do not want to spend all my time on this particular phase of the matter, Mr. Chairman, but before I leave this question I want to point this out. When some of us in this house suggest that some steps could be taken and taken immediately to begin implementing an area of freer trade between the United Kingdom and Canada, there is a place to begin. I think I can give the minister a clue as to where he could begin to the general advantage of all Canadians, regardless of their occupation.
I should like to refer him to a statement made by the commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act when he was reporting upon his investigation into rubber products. This was in 1952, and is to be found at page

683 of that report. After having described the methods by which companies in that field of production had made use of agreements, had conspired to raise the prices of their products unfairly, and had exploited the public to the extent where they were actually breaking the law of Canada, he had this to say, and this is how it is related to our tariff policy:
Another detrimental aspect of the arrangements is related to tariffs. There is substantial tariff protection on most of the products with which the arrangements are concerned. It was of particular significance in respect of certain mechanical rubber goods and tires and tubes. Now when domestic manufacturers are competing behind a tariff barrier, the tariff is serving its intended purpose of protecting the domestic industry against prices from without the country which the domestic industry, in spite of reasonable efficiency, cannot meet or better; and by force of such domestic competition the cost to the consuming public of the tariff protection is minimized. But when domestic prices are set, behind the tariff barrier, by arrangement, then the safeguard provided by competition is absent; the common price tends to be the largest price which the tariff will permit; the cost of the tariff protection to the consuming public is maximized; and, if it is not true that the tariff protection is higher than is actually necessary to protect the domestic industry, the companies privy to the arrangement have at least given the consuming public strong reason to believe that such is the case.
In a word that means there are certain areas of commerce in this country which have been investigated by the officials of the Combines Investigation Act, and it has been found that behind the tariff protection which has been provided for them-perhaps in some cases legitimate protection-they have used that shield of protection to set up monopolies and combines and have exploited the Canadian public through conspiracy to the point of having broken the Canadian law.
In the past the previous government and this government, when they caught up with some of these law-breakers, have taken them to court and after having found, through investigation, that as a result of their combines they have fleeced the public of several million dollars they have whipped them with a reed, fined them $10,000 and told them to go back home and carry on their conspiracy.
That is how effective the Combines Investigation Act has been, but here is a method by which the government could effectively protect the public interest. Where we find that tariff protection is being used for the purpose of forming combines and monopolies and abusing that protection, there is every justification for the government to take immediate action to remove the protection and expose these law-breakers to the effect of an alternative source of supply. Here is a field in which the government could act immediately toward the building up of a free trade area.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
I would now like to refer to the other phase of what I mentioned earlier. That was the complete lack of any reference in the minister's opening speech to the agricultural aspect of his department. Time will not permit me to go into complete detail on this question, and indeed it will not be necessary because several of my colleagues are more qualified than I to go into much greater detail in discussing that particular field, but I do want to draw attention to at least a few of the things that the farm organizations of this country, not only in western Canada but in eastern Canada as well, have considered important enough to have included in their briefs. They have recently sent delegations to the government to present their views to the minister and the cabinet generally. One of those was the brief submitted to the Prime Minister and members of the cabinet on August 15, 1957 by the interprovincial farm union council, which is the co-ordinating body of farm union organizations in, I believe, five provinces at the present time.
Almost the first if indeed not the very first recommendation in that brief, draws attention to the situation with regard to the price of wheat and other grains; and after pointing out that the producers of grain, as a result of the material increase in the cost of production, have not actually been receiving a price for their grain which would bring it anywhere near parity or anywhere near a fair share of the national income, the interprovincial farm union council, as will be found on page 4 of the brief, recommends the following:
1. (a) An immediate interim adjustment payment of 20 cents per bushel on wheat on the 1956-57 crop year deliveries-
That is to be made by the government or by parliament. The recommendation continues:
(b) A payment on oats and barley to bring the net farm prices to producers to a level bearing the same relationship to parity as 20 cents per bushel on wheat.
In other words what they are asking is to have this parliament recognize the fact that the grain producers of this country for a considerable number of years now have been selling their product to the Canadian public and subsidizing the Canadian public by the fact that they are obtaining for their product less than the fair price relationship as between the prices of their products and all prices. They are asking this government to recommend to the house the establishment of an adjustment price or a deficiency payment of 20 cents per bushel on wheat and a proportionately relative amount on oats and barley.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
This is a clear-cut proposition. This is not tied to any long-range plans with regard to any agricultural products. This does not interfere in any way with the Agricultural Prices Support Act or with the proposed resolution which is still gathering moss on the order paper and which the government once in a while brings out, dusts off and txhibits to the house and puts away in mothballs again. It has nothing to do with these things directly. This is a specific proposal and certainly I thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as the minister under whose jurisdiction the Canadian wheat board and therefore the policies of the wheat board come, would have had something to say in connection with this request.
This is a request which concerns many hundreds of thousands of farmers in Canada, but today not a word was said about it. Apparently the minister thought if he ignored it completely perhaps no one else would raise the question and he could quietly get himself out of an awkward spot.

I wish now to refer to something else in the same brief which I consider to be most important and to which the minister made no reference whatsoever. That is the question of marketing boards. There has been a great deal of talk about different methods and means by which we could bring agricultural products including grain up to the level of general prices in this country, or what we generally refer to as a parity price system. One of the methods that has been suggested has been through the payment of adjustment or deficiency payments, or whatever term may be used to describe a payment from the consolidated revenue fund when the prices of farm products fall below parity.
In my opinion, and I am sure that opinion is shared by a great many hon. members in this house, the best method of administering that type of policy if parliament should adopt the parity price policy would be through a system of marketing boards, because there you would have the administrative machinery which would make it possible for this parliament or the treasury to deal with all the farmers who would be part and parcel of the marketing boards, and in that way pay a sufficient amount of money into the funds of the marketing boards when the situation required it so they could

pass it on through what might be called dividends or patronage payments to the farmers Who would sell their products to those boards.
In their proposal concerning this subject the interprovincial farm union council made three or four separate specific recommendations, as will be found on page 16 of their brief, all of which are extremely interesting and important. I regret that the minister had not anything to say about that particular phase of their recommendations today, and I hope he will deal with the subject before this debate is finished.

That is to either pretend that the problem does not exist, or when they do recognize the problem to do nothing but complain about what the United States is doing.
I think the minister will agree that it is time this government found a policy of its own, a policy much more constructive and useful than merely crying about what the government of the United States is doing in the disposal of their surpluses. Mr. Chairman, at the outset of my remarks I would like to congratulate the minister upon taking over the Department of

Trade and Commerce. I wish him every success because it is essential that he be successful; otherwise there may be serious repercussions throughout the country.
The hon. member for Dauphin expressed concern about the minister's department being whittled down. Personally I think it is a good thing that it is being whittled down. I think it should be whittled down to just trade and commerce, because I think trade and commerce are sufficiently important to justify the full time of the minister. As a matter of fact, I think it would be a good thing if grain were taken from the Department of Trade and Commerce and put under agriculture. There is too much overlapping and I would like to see grain brought under the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
When the minister took office he found wheat piled up over the country. I just want to make a few passing references to grain before going on to the general question of trade. As the minister is aware, during the past 10 years grain growers' costs have gone up by 45 per cent, while the price of grain has dropped by 20 per cent. We feel that the immediate need is for an expansion of storage, terminal and off-site, to enable the farmers to deliver more of their grain and, secondly, to have a satisfactory support price under grain because, after all, the grain grower in Canada is the only grain grower in the world who has to take world market prices for his grain. He has to compete not merely with farmers in other countries, he has actually to compete with the treasuries of other countries, and this puts the grain grower of this country in a very difficult position.
This is why I would like to see grain brought under the Agricultural Prices Support Act so that it might be protected under that general formula. If the price of grain were supported under the formula of the Agricultural Prices Support Act it would be around $2.37 today, according to the bureau of statistics; that is, using the base period 1943 to 1945.
Some of my colleagues will be dealing with this matter at greater length and, therefore, I should just like to leave the question of wheat by emphasizing the fact that the only real solution to our grain-marketing problem is the expansion of markets at fair prices. If you accomplish that practically all of the other problems relating to grain will disappear over a period of time.
We look upon the wheat situation as merely a symptom of the weaknesses in our past trade policies. So long as we had a strong sellers' market everything operated satisfactorily. But just as soon as the situation started to toughen up we ran into
Supply-Trade and Commerce difficulty. We have lost many of our markets and I would say that the loss of those markets was due to the rigidity in our trade policies. We had got ourselves into a groove and we were not prepared to get out of that groove and take the action necessary to meet the changing conditions in the world. For example, we have continued the triangular pattern of trade between Great Britain, the United States and Canada. Hon. members will recall that that was outlined back in 1946 by the then minister of finance, when he said-and it can be found at page 764 of Hansard:
We must be able to use the proceeds of our exports to the United Kingdom and the continent of Europe in paying our own bills and debts in the United States.
And that has, generally speaking, been the policy ever since. The former government was very much interested in selling Britain or Europe more goods, but they showed very little interest in bringing imports from Europe into this country. Therefore from time to time we have had protests from various ministers from Great Britain pointing out that unless Canada was prepared to achieve a greater degree of balance with that country it would not be possible for Britain to expand her imports from this country. For instance, just last year when Sir Anthony Eden was over here he is reported by the Ottawa Journal of February 7, 1956, as follows:
Prime Minister Sir Anthony Eden told a press conference today that the imbalance in trade between Canada and the United Kingdom-two to one in favour of Canada-must be rectified if that trade is to continue growing.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we think it is very important to depart from that triangular pattern of trade and recognize the fact that trade is a two-way street. If we want other nations to buy from us we have to buy from them and do everything we can to establish a balance of trade. I think the present situation is one that calls for a good deal of concern. We had an adverse balance of trade with the U.S.A. last year of $1,283 million; with the world, $842 million; with the United Kingdom, a favourable balance of trade of $333 million. We used that $333 million, of course, to help pay the adverse balance of trade with the U.S.A.
There are some people who ask, why should we worry about an imbalance of trade? We have investments from the United States of America, and those investments will pay the losses suffered under the adverse balance of trade. It is interesting to remember that an increase in foreign investment invariably means an increase in your adverse balance of trade. The reason is obvious. Firms
