Supply-Trade and Commerce in this country, and especially firms with parent companies in the United States, obtain their funds from the United States and they invariably spend a large portion of those funds in the United States to bring goods into this country, and the more investment there is by the United States the greater will be the imbalance of trade.
I was interested in a statement made by the chairman of A. V. Roe (Canada) Limited, as quoted in the Ottawa Journal of October 25, 1957, regarding this adverse balance of trade. He said:
"You have only to glance at Canada's staggering trade deficit with the United States", Sir Roy said in an address to the Roe annual meeting, "to see
where opportunities lie.
This represents a serious problem for Canada but it also offers a rare oportunity to Canadian industry.
In that vast deficit (of more than $1 billion annually) there must be many millions of dollars worth of products that can and should be made in tii s country.
Canada must produce more of the products which she uses and which she now imports. Your population is increasing by 1 million every 30 months

one of the highest rates of growth in the world. If this is to be maintained, and it must be if Canada is to grow, then more and more new jobs must be found".
It is interesting to note that at the very time that statement was made we had around 208,000 unemployed in Canada. I believe the figure is greater than that today.
Of course these unemployed could be used to produce many of the goods to which Sir Roy Dobson has reference in his speech.
I think it is very unfortunate that at the very time when we have this large adverse balance of trade and it is so essential that we should increase the production in Canada of goods which we import from the United States the Bank of Canada decided to impose restrictions on the expansion of credit that had the effect of reducing the rate of our production because there was never a time when we should have expanded our production more than now, at the time we have this large adverse balance of trade. There is good reason to say that we should have used the surplus labour we had to expand the production of those goods which at the present time we are importing from the United States.
I think everybody will agree that the logical solution of the problem of imbalance of trade is either to sell more to the United States or to buy less from them. It is not so easy to sell more unless the United States is willing to buy more, but on the other hand we have control over the other aspect and could buy less. We could either do that, as Sir Roy Dobson suggests, by expanding our production of those things which we are at present buying from the United States, and of course that would be the desirable thing
[Mr. Quelch.j

to do, or otherwise we could buy less by purchasing certain goods we are buying from the United States from countries with which we have a favourable balance of trade.
Therefore I was very glad to see the government send a mission to the United Kingdom to try to expand our purchases in that country, and I am not going to be too critical of it being a buying mission. If we want to sell more to the United Kingdom we have got to buy more. In view of the fact that we have had a substantial favourable balance of trade for a number of years, the first thing is to rectify that by buying more and I believe, as I think the minister has suggested, that if we can create a situation where we buy enough from Britain to bring about a balance of trade then Britain will be willing to buy more from us. When Sir Anthony Eden was in Canada last year he stressed the fact that if Canada would buy more from Britain that country would buy more from us and desires to do so. Therefore I think we are doing the logical thing. We are first of all trying to balance trade with Britain by buying more from them and we have every reason to believe that if we accomplish that Britain will then buy more from us.
We have always insisted that nations should endeavour to bring about the greatest degree of balance in their trade with other nations on a bilateral basis. I recall that every time I suggested that in the house in the past the former minister of trade and commerce used to ridicule the idea. He would say that it was nonsense to suggest having a balance of trade bilaterally, that it had to be on a multilateral basis. It is a fine thing to have a balance on a multilateral basis but if you cannot the first thing to do is to try to achieve the greatest degree of balance on a bilateral basis. I recall that the former deputy minister of trade and commerce emphasized that fact back in 1947. Mr. M. W. Mackenzie in an article in the Foreign Trade magazine of October 9, 1947, had this to say:
Now that the multilateral system of payments has suffered a serious breakdown for the second time, or perhaps one should say for the third time in the last generation, Canada and all other countries that are engaged heavily in international trade are facing a difficult stage in their affairs. The balance of trade between pairs of countries-that is, the bilateral balance-has become a matter of first importance and it will remain so until the mechanism of the multilateral system has once more been placed in good order.
We were never able to convince the former minister of trade and commerce that that was an objective worth trying to achieve but the former deputy minister, who has been spoken of very highly in the house, I know, considered it advisable in these difficult times.

Times were difficult then and so far as our imbalance of trade is concerned they are even more difficult today.
So, as I say, I am very glad to see that the government at least is trying to achieve that degree of balance bilaterally in so far as the United Kingdom is concerned. If by transferring some of our purchases from the) United States to Britain we are able to make it possible for Britain to achieve a balance of trade with us, it will also help us to achieve a greater degree of balance with the United States. In other words, we would be killing two birds with one stone and we would be departing from that triangular pattern of trade that in my opinion has done so much to lose us markets in the United Kingdom.
I think it is time that we raised international trade to its true purpose, the exchange of goods are services between nations of a mutually advantageous character. I think we should be prepared to accept foreign currency in payment for our exports up to the amount of our favourable balance of trade with any nation under a firm agreement to spend it on the nation's goods and services or trade the credit to another nation. Some hon. members will recall that in 1945 we had a prolonged debate on the Bretton Woods agreement. The Bretton Woods agreement gave creditor nations the right to demand payment in their own currency without any obligation whatsoever to accept goods of the importing nation. We stressed then that if that type of policy should continue one of two things was bound to happen. Either the debtor nation, the importing nation, would be forced to go farther and farther into debt to the exporting nation or they would be forced to curtail imports from the creditor nation. At that time when we were debating the bill in the banking and commerce committee I put the matter in these words as found on page 131 of the proceedings of that committee:
What we want in the act mainly is a provision that a debtor nation in order to pay for its imports shall be recognized as paying for them when they establish a credit within their country in favour of a creditor nation and that that credit can be used to buy anything purchased within that country. Then if the creditor nation is not willing to accept goods from a nation with which it has a credit, if it desires to trade on a multilateral basis it may take the credit established on that basis for the credit of another country on a multilateral basis. So I say if the great industrialized nations are really sincere in this matter they should have shown it at this time and been willing to have an article to that effect put in the Bretton Woods agreement.
Unfortunately, however, that was not done. We continued on the basis of the triangular pattern of trade and as a consequence we have lost many of our markets in Europe, not because those nations do not desire to buy
Supply-Trade and Commerce from us but because they lack the dollars for the very simple reason that we insist upon exporting more goods to them than we are willing to buy from them. Once again I say I think we are on the right track when we try to expand our purchases from the sterling area.
No one is suggesting that the Canadian exporter should have to accept sterling. We realize that the individual exporter cannot accept sterling. I should imagine the procedure would be that the exporter would draw bills in sterling on the British importer, discount them with his local bank and the bank would then discount them with the federal agency. The federal agency would then have a claim against sterling and would be able to make that sterling available to Canadian importers of British goods. We have consistently urged in the house the acceptance of inconvertible sterling. It is no good accepting ordinary sterling because if you are going to accept what is known as American account sterling it probably means you will be converting that sterling back into dollars and you might as well have taken dollars in the first place. What we think should be done is that there should be an agreement to accept sterling from Britain under the firm undertaking that that sterling will be used to buy goods of that nation. If that is done, I think we will find Britain is far more interested in our accepting inconvertible sterling than they are in our accepting American account sterling which may be converted at any time or on any day into dollars.
The former minister of trade and commerce and the former minister of finance were very much opposed to the idea of the acceptance of sterling. As a matter of fact, I remember earlier they used to try to ridicule the suggestion. They continued ridiculing the idea until the United States put into force their surplus disposal policy. They were then very critical of the United States for initiating such a program, and criticized it time and again. I understand that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce also is somewhat critical of the United States disposal policy.
I do not believe we really have any grounds for being critical of the United States in putting that policy into force. I feel it is time we broadened our policies out along somewhat similar lines. May I remind the minister of the background of United States surplus disposal programs? The minister may recall that back in 1948 or 1949 surpluses were starting to cause a great deal of concern. This matter had been referred to the Food and Agriculture Organization. The director general of the Food and Agriculture

Supply-Trade and Commerce Organization then appointed a committee of six experts to draft proposals for handling surpluses, and ways and means by which those surpluses might be distributed to other nations. These experts come up with a proposal known as the international commodity clearing house.
I want to draw the minister's attention to the functions of that clearing house because what the United States is doing today is along very similar lines. It is interesting to note that these proposals were rejected by the member nations. They were advised that one of the reasons the proposals should be rejected was that each nation could put the financial proposals into force themselves without having an international commodity clearing house. Let the minister note what the functions of that international commodity clearing house would have been. Mind you, these were proposals drawn up by a committee of experts under the director general of the Food and Agriculture Organization. The functions were:
(1)	Subject to provisions outlined below, the purchase of stocks of commodities that are in surplus in the country in which those stocks appear.
(2)	The negotiation of sales in inconvertible currencies in order to assist in maintaining the flow of trade during periods of exchange disequilibrium; such payments being guaranteed by the buying countries against losses from exchange depreciation.
(3)	The negotiation of sales at special prices below the market to countries in need, under strictly defined conditions of use; for example, for relief purposes, special nutritional programs, or for development projects.
(4)	As a long run function, the holding of stocks acquired in periods of surplus as reserves to protect the interests of consumers in periods of shortage.
(5)	The negotiation of bilateral or multilateral trading agreements, or exchanges of commodities on a barter basis.
The minister will note that these functions outlined for the international commodity clearing house are the very things that the United States today are doing under their disposal program. As I say, at the time this program was turned down by the member nations of FAO they had been advised of a number of reasons why it should be turned down. Under paragraph (d), we find:
That the financial functions proposed for the international commodity clearing house could be performed by the governments directly involved.
The United States was one of the governments involved. The United States are today doing the very thing they were advised could be done by member nations of the Food and Agriculture Organization. I do not feel, therefore, we are in a very good position to criticize the United States for doing what they are doing today. I would suggest that instead of criticizing the United States what we should do is adopt whatever features


there are in that policy that might be advantageous to this country. I believe we could very well accept inconvertible currencies from any nation to the extent necessary to provide for balancing trade with that nation. I am not suggesting we go beyond that. If we are agreed that it should be the purpose of international trading to exchange goods and services upon a basis of mutual advantage, then surely we should be willing either to balance our trade with nations or accept their currency to the extent necessary to provide that balance. We would thus remove a lot of the annoyances that are so often created between nations.
As an alternative to accepting foreign currency or sterling, I think we should be prepared to make advances of credit through the Bank of Canada to purchasing nations for the purchase of Canadian goods. The purchasing nation would be under an obligation to give Canada a prior claim on its exportable production, but should be required only to retire the advance of credit at the rate and to the extent Canada chooses to exercise its claim against the exportable goods. In other words, Canada would not have the right to demand payment in dollars. On the other hand, she would be free to exchange the credits for goods of another nation with which the debtor nation has a favourable balance of trade. Of course, the importing nation should be prepared to guarantee the rate of exchange on their currency.
As I have already stated, I think the government is to be commended for their effort to do something about the serious imbalance of trade by reducing our purchases from the United States and expanding our purchases from the sterling area. But I think most people will agree that probably that is a very long-term program. I noticed one of the British officials says there is no reason why it would not be possible to expand British purchases to $1 billion. This would be getting along pretty close to the objective of the Prime Minister, but it was pointed out that that may take many years. I feel we could expedite this matter by being willing to accept a certain amount of inconvertible sterling.
I hope the minister will not just brush it aside like the former minister. He must realize the people of the United States are good businessmen. They look upon this as good business. They are not doing it because it is philanthropic. They are doing it because they think it is good business for themselves. Let us remember it is having this effect. It is making surplus food available to the hungry people of the world and that, in itself,

is certainly a worth-while objective. At the same time, under the United States program, the farmer who produces that surplus food is getting fair prices. I hope the minister will give greater consideration to that program.

Mr. Chairman, I was very much interested this morning in the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I listened to him with a great deal of attention. I regretted that he did not give us the forecasts we used to be given by the former minister of trade and commerce when he outlined the trading position of our country and gave us his views on the expansion of industry, as well as the amount of capital that would be invested. In other words, during the presentation of the estimates of this department we had a forecast of Canadian trade for some considerable time in the future. The minister in his wisdom or otherwise neglected to do that this morning. I regretted it, and I listened with a great deal of attention to his statement. I have not found very much in it that one could take home and think about. As a matter of fact the only commendable thing I could find about this statement was that it was so brief.
There is one part of the statement by the minister with which I agree and that was his tribute paid to the staff of his department, built up I might say by years of Liberal administration. I have had experience with the staff of this department and can readily agree with the minister when he pays tribute to their earnest efforts both at home and abroad. He said in effect that the purpose of the trade commissioners' service is to advance Canadian export trade and he also paid tribute to the personnel of that service. Then if this is correct, and I believe it to be correct as I believe the minister to be sincere in his tribute, why the necessity of sending the trade mission to England since we have such an efficient staff already over there which can inform the trade of Great Britain as to our requirements.
Now I understand statements have been made by the right hon. Prime Minister and other members of the government that it is the intention to transfer 15 per cent of our imports from the United States to Great Britain. Now to be fair I think that is a commendable idea but if the policy of this government is anti-United States to that extent it also raises a great deal of fears in my mind. I have no objection to transferring 15 per cent of this trade from the United States to Great Britain if we are not killing ourselves in the process.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Let us look at this trade position from a commonsense standpoint. First of all may I say that the people of Great Britain are not going to buy from Canada or anywhere else if they can buy cheaper elsewhere. We in Newfoundland have been trading with Great Britain for hundreds of years and we understand their trading position and know how they trade. I have a situation in my riding which is rather unusual and perhaps may be of interest to the members of this house and to the people of Canada. We had an unusual ice blockade around our coast this year. This does happen once in a while, and because of this tremendous blockade our national industry was interfered with. When I refer to our national industry I mean, of course, our fisheries industry which was affected to such an extent that our lobster fishing failed in large part, our salmon fishing failed and our cod fishing, which is our main fish product, was also interfered with. This brought about a rather serious condition in the fishing industry in a large part of Newfoundland, particularly in my own riding.
Now our fishermen, who usually give up the voyage either in the months of August or September when they go, as we say, into the lumber woods and work through September, October, November and December coming home for Christmas and thereby earning sufficient to provide for their needs and those of their families during the winter, were faced with a different situation. We have been exporting thousands of cords of pulp-wood to Great Britain for the last 20 years and some of us on this side of the house agreed with the Conservative party when they said we should process our own raw material in this country. We have two large paper mills in Newfoundland but we have never begrudged Great Britain buying this material from us because we wanted to help them. This year, just as our fishermen were preparing to go into the lumber woods to earn their daily bread for the winter, we were informed by one of the large paper companies -the larger of the two in Newfoundland- that they had laid off 700 men, thus adding to our rather serious unemployment situation. When they were asked why they were not exporting this pulpwood to Great Britain -let it be understood that we exported this material during the war and at other times to help the paper industry of Great Britain and have made no complaint about it-we were informed that Great Britain was buying the pulpwood elsewhere. When we asked why they were doing so we were promptly told Great Britain could get it cheaper elsewhere.

Mr. Chairman, may I take this opportunity, when the house is taking up the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, to pay particular tribute to Mr. C. D. Howe, that great economist. I can speak out of personal knowledge for when I first went into business, I scrupulously applied his wise counsels to industrialists and Canadian financiers who were promoting the development of their plants or business, either by expanding or by the purchase of equipment, thus automatically furthering the economic expansion of this country. That is why I say that I am indebted to Mr. Howe for at least part of the success I have enjoyed.
I frankly admit that I have always looked upon Mr. Howe's statements as a barometer and a guide when I was planning my course at the beginning of any particular fiscal year. I am sure that a large number of Canadian businessmen set great store by his annual forecast which incidentally, never failed to come true.
How utterly different under this new government. A curious fact is that for all their bombastic statements and confident outlook, the new ministers by no means are inspiring the same degree of confidence as did the leaders of the great Liberal party. Hence the worry, nervousness, uncertainty, restlessness and weariness that grip the people of Canada.
No more striking example of this could be found than in my own constituency where our industrialists have not only expressed

Supply-Trade and Commerce concern but have protested in unequivocal fashion against the attitude of the present government.
Let me name but one large firm in my district, the Bennett Company Limited, of Chambly, which has forwarded a brief to the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Finance in Ottawa setting out its worries and concern. This submission reads as follows:
(Text):
We believe that the government is making a tremendous mistake in not protecting Canadian industry.
"Free trade" cannot be considered with England or any other country when their standard of wages are not comparable with Canadian standards. It is impossible for Canadian companies to pay $1.50 an hour compared to 50 cents an hour in England and have the resulting products competitive in price.
(Translation):
The firm admits that it is all very well to say we should buy British goods but wonders whether Canada can compete with England when wages for the same classes of employment are $1.50 an hour here and 50 cents over there.
Our government must change their attitude and policy as far as our imports from England are concerned. The situation demands a very serious study on the part of Canadian authorities. As suggested by the Bennett Company, if the government want at all cost to promote the employment of Canadian labour, they must take a quite different stand and clearly side with Canadian industry.
When our manufacturers are no longer able to stand the competition of imported goods, an economic depression will set in. Our industries will shut down and our workers will be unemployed. Imported shoes, for instance, will still be available at $4 or $5 a pair, but the worker will not have the money to buy them. I would rather pay ten or twelve dollars for a pair of shoes, and have the money to buy them, and at the same time avoid a depression such as we had in the thirties, under another unlamented and Conservative government.
A further suggestion appears appropriate to me in another field. The government should co-operate with companies such as the Canadian Industries Limited in carrying out a vast program of scientific research.
After all this company, as many others of the same type, spends huge amounts each year on research aimed at finding new markets for new or better products. Those master chemists and scientists contribute to the expansion of our industries and, by their knowledge, can help solve many problems.
Let me make still another suggestion as to how the wheat problem in western Canada might be solved.

This $150,000,000 program put into effect by the present government in seeking to settle the acute problem of the disposal of wheat is designed to provide the western farmer with interest free cash advances.
May I say that this measure can only be a stopgap. True, the cash advances provided to the individual farmer will run as high as $3,000 but this will in no way dispose of the enormous quantities of wheat accumulated in storage.
I would like to bring my modest contribution to the solution of this problem. Why not set up an agency which would undertake research to discover new by-products of wheat? After all, if it has been found that wood can be used to manufacture paper, why should not wheat be used to manufacture new products?
As far as the constituency of Chambly-Rouville is concerned, I would like to bring to the attention of my colleagues the possibilities offered by that federal constituency.
Now don't think this is just another wholly agricultural county of our province. It is, indeed, an agricultural county, but because of its geographical position, it is a district which also occupies a strategic position in the great triangle that is developing as a consequence of the St. Lawrence Seaway project. Situated along the southern bank of our majestic river, and south of the Canadian metropolis of Montreal, the county of Chambly-Rouville is a hive of residential and industrial projects.
This brings me to point out to the Conservative government that those great projects must absolutely be continued, particularly after the Liberal government has set the foundations of unequalled economic development.
When you read the history of the United States,-and you will recall that a former Liberal leader once said that the 20th century "belongs to Canada",-you realize the tremendous development which has occurred in that great country, particularly in that corner of San Francisco which is referred to as "the Golden Gate". Well, Mr. Chairman, the district which I have the honour to represent here will be named the "Golden Triangle of Canada". The district extending from Beauharnois to St. Johns and from St. Johns to Sorel is indeed the "Golden Triangle". This will occur, of course, provided the Liberal party is brought back into power, so that it may keep on giving this country this era of prosperity which used to be ours, because at this time, the Conservative party is merely engaged in electoral overbidding, thus destroying the economy of the country, after having sabotaged national unity. It is most unfortunate that, after dealing a first

nasty blow at national unity by holding that his party can manage the affairs of Canada without the help of the province of Quebec, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) should now get down to sabotaging Canadian economy by clinging to an obsolete imperialistic feeling which would alienate the friendship of the United States, whose economic contribution to our Canadian development has, up to now, been a tremendous asset.
The Canadian people can rightfully regret its old love, the Liberal party.

Mr. Chairman, I did not have the opportunity to speak during the debate on the speech from the throne but I think this would be an appropriate time for me to express my opinion on matters which affect Lincoln county, the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and which in a general way affect all parts of Canada.
Canada's most unfavourable trade balance with the United States and other countries coupled with our tremendous surplus of farm produce was one of the main reasons that brought about the change of government on June 10. This condition was created by the disorderly importation into this country of manufactured goods at prices with which our factories could not compete and the dumping of surplus farm products from the United States into Canada at prices below cost. The loss of world markets for our farm products was also a very important factor in this slump in the farming industry. I fully realize that there are many problems the Minister of Trade and Commerce has to solve in order to correct some of those conditions. If we examine the records of trade and commerce we find that imports and exports between Canada and the United States represent the area wherein most of our problems lie.
I firmly believe that at least 15 per cent of our trade with the United States can be diverted to Great Britain in the purchase of heavy machinery and equipment much of which is not made in Canada at the present time. This exchange should be based on Great Britain's purchasing in return a further 15 per cent more in terms of farm products under a trade agreement which I am sure this government can easily negotiate with the British government.
Turning now to the problem that faces Canada's light industries including textiles, small tools, hardware, etc., something must be done in the very near future to offer them assistance. If action is not taken soon there will not be a textile plant left in Ontario. Our chief competitors in textiles are Japan 96698-126J
Supply-Trade and Commerce and West Germany. Both countries purchase a considerable amount of Canadian wheat and therefore we cannot disturb that trade too much. However, their exports to Canada are increasing rapidly and our exports to those countries are not increasing at the same rate. We do not wish to discontinue trading with any country, but in these days, when every country seems to be extending its markets, we do not want to be caught short, which we have been. The only way we can possibly protect ourselves today is by trade agreements.
How can Canada compete with Japan on an almost open market like the Canadian market today? I am told that the pay of semi-skilled and skilled labour is from 50 cents to 60 cents a day. In Ontario people performing the same job are paid from $1.25 to $2.50 an hour, with compensation, unemployment insurance, holiday pay and, in most factories where they are covered by union agreements, they have sick pay, life insurance, hospitalization, Physicians' Services Incorporated and, in some cases, a guaranteed annual wage. We have them all. Most of those measures are unknown in some of those countries I have mentioned.
During the last four years of the Liberal government, Lincoln county, the county I represent, lost four good textile plants with a payroll of some 1,200 people. My opponents in the last election said, "What of it?"

I might say that I was down in the province of Quebec and visited the town of Vic-toriaville where we go quite often. They used to have a very fine plywood mill down there. They have two of the largest furniture factories in Canada and they used the plywood from their own mills. The last time I was down there that factory also was shut down.
Small tools is another item that affects Ontario. We have a number of plants in St. Catharines which are manufacturing small tools. We find today that in order to maintain their sales staff and keep their markets some of those plants are having their products manufactured in West Germany, brought out to this country and sold under their own brand names. That is not a good condition. I do not say that we can cure it all at once but it is just the trend of things today. We are buying too much from abroad and causing unemployment in our own country.
When we were discussing fisheries the other day it was brought out that at the present time we are importing large quantities of salmon from Japan. I checked that and I found that most of that salmon is caught just outside of territorial waters. It is processed in floating canneries and some of it never even sees Japan.
In closing, sir, I must say that our government must approach this whole problem of agriculture and light industry with a realistic and a sympathetic attitude. It must keep in mind the fact that it was Canada's trade deficit of $1,300 million and our depressed agricultural industry that brought so many new members like myself to Ottawa. Mr. Chairman, I wish at the outset to join with those who have wished the Minister of Trade and Commerce every success in his office. I think we all realize the importance of this department, since it affects the daily life of every Canadian citizen. It is unfortunate that the minister took office at a time when there is a shadow caused by the problems arising out of the international investment position. There are several suggestions which I should like to make in this regard and in other aspects dealing with the minister's department. I want


to emphasize the international investment position and in doing so I am not putting any blame on the present administration; nor do I think that blame can be put on the former administration because we, as Canadians, are all to blame for allowing the situation to develop.
I would draw to the attention of hon. members a publication put out by the dominion bureau of statistics entitled, "Canada's International Investment Position, 1926-1954". It provides an analysis of the trends which have built up over the years and I think that our immediate responsibility is that of analysing those trends and determining corrective measures which will stop the trend if, in our opinion, we feel it is not in the best interests of the people of this country.
I think it is important to note that two of the measures which this government has already adopted are aimed at correcting the trend. I think the one which came into being first was the commonwealth conference, and we are hopeful that it will achieve its objective of diverting more of our trade from countries where we have an imbalance to countries where we have a credit. The present trade commission, which is currently touring the United Kingdom, can play a very valuable role and we wish it success in achieving that end.
I think it is particularly important that this be given consideration, in view of the developments which are taking place in continental Europe, such as the development of the free-trade area which will in all probability make our trading relations with those countries somewhat more difficult and adjustments must be made on our behalf.
In reference to the imbalance of our international trading position, I should like to quote from the publication to which I referred. It says:
Non-resident ownership of Canadian manufacturing now amounts to about a half of the total capital employed and to well over a half in the case of mining, smelting and petroleum.
I think all hon. members will readily agree that it is a very dangerous trend to have foreign capital taking ownership and control of some of our basic industries. It is understandable, of course, that in the period through which Canada has gone a certain amount of risk capital should come into the country, but I am also certain that we as Canadians must put ourselves in a position to be able to exercise sufficient control over this foreign investment to ensure that in fact we do control the industries that exist in

Canada. The publication goes on to state the following respecting these concerns controlled in the United States:
These larger concerns, with an investment of $1 million or more, accounted for some 30 per cent of Canadian manufacturing production in 1953 and 21 per cent of employment in that field.
There we have an insight into the implications that have developed in the first half of this century through allowing foreign concerns to control in fact many of our Canadian industries. As foreign capital achieves greater control of industry operating in Canada, this in turn makes it more difficult for private individuals to establish themselves in the manufacturing field since they are competing against large concerns with limitless amounts of capital.
This is particularly significant in the automobile industry. Ninety-eight per cent of the Canadian automotive industry is dominated by large United States controlled enterprises. This thought went through my mind last Monday when we were discussing the plight of the industry due to lay-offs resulting from the uncertainty of buyers as to reduction of the excise tax on automobiles. It seemed to me that perhaps these United States concerns were closing down their Canadian plants in an effort to use this action as a lever against the Canadian government to reduce the tax and thus provide the industry with an advantage which they were not prepared to provide for themselves through a reduction in the price of their product.
I should point out too that the rubber industry is another that is largely controlled in the United States, as are the petroleum, iron and machinery industries. I am just mentioning them and I am not going to go into a great amount of detail because it is a very technical subject. However, I wish to draw this very serious trend to the minister's attention, a trend that exists at a time when we have an imbalance of trade with the United States. Of course, the imbalance has been covered over the years by capital inflow, both in direct and indirect investments. The deficiency last year amounted to over $1 billion, and as we continue to import more from the United States than we export to that country this situation is offset by a larger inflow of United States capital which in turn aggravates our problem by creating more and more domination of our industries by a foreign power.
I hope the minister will give these factors serious consideration and do everything possible to halt and reverse this trend. It is important that this be done because of the tremendous changes that have taken place in the whole pattern of international trade since the war.
Supply-Trade and Commerce The hon. member for Acadia, in a very sensible speech as usual, remarked on the change in the trade pattern that had taken place. He pointed out that we no longer have the multilateral trade which existed from the turn of the century up to world war II when Great Britain was the clearing house and trade was channelled in a multilateral way. As an individual country we must now concentrate on unilateral and bilateral trade agreements and, again keeping the emphasis on Canada's international investment position, it will be necessary to establish import-export boards so that our trade will be in useful channels and in commodities which are in fact necessary in Canada.
It has been said many times and should be said many times that we can sell to countries only if we are prepared to buy from them. I think I should again draw attention here to the very serious omission in the opening remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the complete omission of any reference to what was termed by the Prime Minister during the election campaign as Canada's No. 1 problem, our tremendous wheat surplus. It is part and parcel of the whole problem of trade. For years wheat was our major export commodity. It has dropped in recent years to second or third place but it is still of extreme importance to the people of western Canada and, in fact, all of Canada.
The fact that we have a billion bushels of wheat in public and private storage is indeed an important consideration directly related to international trade. In my opinion it is necessary to follow trade policies that will give consideration to this problem. This will require the importation from countries which are in a position to buy from us of sufficient goods to provide them with funds with which they in turn can purchase our grain. If difficulties do arise, as in fact they do, I think serious consideration should be given to barter arrangements to permit countries that do not have the required amount of dollars to make direct trades with our country.
I recall asking the minister if consideration had been given to having the trade mission currently touring Great Britain discuss this problem and he pointed out that consideration had not been given to barter arrangements because it was not found necessary. When we have a billion bushels of wheat in storage I think it is necessary to give consideration to barter arrangements. It is necessary to give consideration to long-term credit agreements so that this wheat, which is a glut on the Canadian economy, can move into foreign markets.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
This will also require consideration of the acceptance of foreign currencies. Failing the adoption of these programs with respect to international trade, we then have the responsibility of launching domestic programs to take care of the existing situation. If we are not going to have trade policies that will enable our wheat to move freely into the marketing channels of the world, the responsibility must fall on the government to provide policies that will enable the farmers to exist. I know that some of my colleagues will be dealing further with this subject and I do not want to labour the point now because it will be gone into in more detail on the specific items in the minister's estimates.
But I would point out that one solution that could be adopted would be to increase the amount of grain in storage on which storage charges are paid. The previous administration introduced legislation to provide for the payment of storage charges by the federal government on all grain in excess of 178 million bushels. I am completely in the dark as to how the figure of 178 million bushels was arrived at, but I would suggest that they take that figure out and pay the storage charges on all grain which is, in fact, in storage. Consideration must be given also to the application of programs to benefit all farmers, the ones which were mentioned by my colleague the hon. member for Dauphin in the form of deficiency payments; the adoption of the two-price system and the payment of storage to farmers on farm-held grain.
I have dealt, rather hurriedly I must admit, with some of the aspects of the trade of our country. I should like now to make reference to two specific problems relative to the commerce of our country. I am quite certain that the minister will be in a position to more readily correct these problems than ones to which I referred previously. I am the father of three children, and on occasion I have been sent by my wife to buy a pair of jeans for one of the boys. I arrive at the department store and look for a size 6. When I find one that seems to be satisfactory I bring it home. Often I find that it would very easily fit my 8-year old daughter. On the other hand, I may find a similar garment, take it home and I might be lucky if it fits my 4-year old son. Apparently, Mr. Chairman, there is a complete lack of standardization in the quality and style of children's clothes. I am bringing this to the minister's attention because I have received many complaints from mothers across Canada. We can appreciate the difficulty they have in getting away to shop for their families, and I think steps should be taken

to standardize the sizes of children's clothes. All garments marked "Size 6" should be the same size, and then when we hapless fathers are sent out on a shopping errand we would have more guidance in the selection of these articles.
The second item about which I should like to complain and draw to the attention of the house is this miserable practice which has been developing in recent months of pressure merchandising. The practice seems to be to stuff all kinds of toys and objects in these so-called breakfast cereals. I have been out shopping with my children and I have been coerced, cajoled, cried at and commanded to buy certain brands of breakfast cereal just for the purpose of obtaining the marble, jet airplane or toy pistol inside the package. I believe controls could be exercised to prevent this merciless pressure being put on the parents of Canada. It is very difficult for parents who are with their families to turn down the request of the children who want the toys far more than the breakfast cereal. The result is that you have dozens of boxes of breakfast cereal cluttering up the closet which the children do not want. If someone has a secret on how to say no, I wish they would let me in on it.
Equally bad, but not with the same devastating result, is the practice of placing premiums in packaged goods. The best example of this practice might be the packaged soaps. You find a huge box of soap, you buy it and find it is filled with a bath size tea towel or bath size beach towel, with a small quantity of soap at the bottom. I would not mind having a bath size tea towel, at that. I think regulations should be invoked to protect the housewives all across Canada from this type of pressure advertising. I believe that this would come under the jurisdiction of the department of commerce.
I have one final suggestion. I am making a plea on behalf of the small merchants throughout the length and breadth of Canada that we get rid of these premium coupons. This practice may be all right for the large merchants who have the capacity to deal with these coupons, but the small merchant does not have a filing system for keeping these coupons until the salesman happens to come around. What happens is that the small merchant is bearing the cost of the premium which is offered by the soap company or whatever company it may be. If the manufacturers do, in fact, want to provide an incentive, let them reduce the price of their commodity by 5 or 10 cents. In this way the individual merchant will not be saddled with these onerous responsibilities.

Mr. Chairman, I think I am rather familiar with this bill because it arises out of certain expropriations by the St. Lawrence seaway authority during the time when I was president of that corporation. I should like to preface my answer to my hon. friend with a brief statement about the manner in which the bill comes before the house. The New York Central Railway operates from Ottawa to a point near Rooseveltown in the state of New York. The plans of the St. Lawrence seaway authority and the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation, the
Private Bills
United States entity building the seaway, provided for a loop over Cornwall island at substantial cost.
When the St. Lawrence seaway authority looked at the plans they discovered that instead of following that loop and relocating the railway they could follow a straight line and save a considerable amount of money by purchasing the line from Cornwall to Rooseveltown. It also appeared during the course of the study of these plans that the New York Central railway was considering the abandonment of the line because of the fact there was little or no freight traffic over the line. It is well known that in the last few years there has been no passenger service between either Rooseveltown or Cornwall and the city of Ottawa and just one freight service per week, but what prompted the New York Central railway to give consideration to the whole matter of sale and abandonment was the fact that two companies in the United States had invited the New York Central to give them certain freight concessions if they established themselves on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river.
In view of all the circumstances the St. Lawrence seaway authority and St. Lawrence seaway development corporation decided to purchase this railway from Rooseveltown to Cornwall and an application was then made to the board of transport commissioners. The board thereafter approved of the application to discontinue and abandon the line but not until after a similar application had been made by the New York Central railway before the inter-state commerce commission in the United States, and granted by them.
Now dealing with the question raised by my hon. friend with respect to the employees who were affected I understand that by virtue of a section of the Railway Act it is possible for employees to make certain representations to the board for compensation. The employees did this and the board, by virtue of one of the sections of the act, referred these representations to the Supreme Court of Canada. I understand that the Supreme Court of Canada made a ruling on the question to which the hon. gentleman has referred and which, I am sorry to say, was not favourable to the employees of the New York Central railway.

Then he showed how the acreage has fluctuated for these two grains. With regard to flax, within the last 10 years or so the acreage has doubled. I am not sure whether he indicated that with regard to rye

the acreage has been correspondingly reduced. The acreage for rye is about one-fifth of what it was 10 years ago.
I notice that these two crops in seeded acreage are about one-tenth of the great crops of western Canada, wheat, oats and barley, which are under the wheat board at the present time. There are other seeded crops which the hon. member who has introduced this bill might at some time or other also wish to bring under the wheat board. However, he has concentrated his attention at the present time on these two and has indicated that there is a considerable demand among the farmers of western Canada for the bringing of flax and rye under the wheat board.
However, I notice that in supporting his argument-and I quote now from page 438 of Hansard-he indicated to the house the extent of the interest of the western farmer by these words:
I may say that I wrote to every municipality in the province of Saskatchewan and the replies I received to the question whether or not they were in favour of the inclusion of flax and rye under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board were practically unanimous.
When I heard that, as I listened to the debates and when I read it again I wondered whether the hon. member could be a little more exact in his argument here in order that the argument might be stronger than it appears at the moment. He says that he wrote to every municipality. Well, we accept that. Then, he goes on to say: "The replies I received". He does not indicate whether he had two replies or 100 replies, or whether he heard from every municipality to which he wrote. He says that the replies were practically unanimous, which means that some were opposed. In any case, to whom were these questions addressed? He says he wrote to every municipality. Were they addressed to the secretaries of the municipalities? Did the questions come before the reeve and the councillors and who gave the reply? Did the reply come by way of an indication from the reeve and the council? Were the replies the personal opinions of the secretary-treasurers of the municipalities? Were the actual farmers approached in the matter? I thought that in the course of a very able speech the hon. member for Moose Mountain might have been somewhat more exact with regard to that particular matter if he wished us to accept it as a strong argument in favour of bringing flax and rye under the wheat board.
Now, I do not question for one minute the importance of this subject. But during the course of the summer two presentations were made to the cabinet, one of which was made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture on
Canadian Wheat Board Act July 31, 1957. I have read this through with care on more than one occasion and, unless my memory is failing me at the moment, I do not recall that the subject matter of flax and rye formed part of that submission of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. If it is as important to the farmers of western Canada as the hon. member for Moose Mountain suggests to us I would have thought that in the submission made to us by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture some mention would have been made of these two grains. They did deal with the subject of grain and they did deal with the question of wheat, and so on, but I do not see flax and rye mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, the Department of Finance estimates as printed in the blue book show an increase in the amount to be voted this year over last year of just over $10 million. If the details are examined, however, it will be seen that more than all this increase is covered by two kinds of grants- grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes and grants to universities. Apart from these two sets of grants we are asking parliament to vote slightly less money than was required a year ago for the administration of this department.
I should, however, in this opening statement take into consideration not only the main estimates but also the supplementaries of both years. The principal large item in this year's supplementaries is $32 million for the general salaries vote. This is more than offset however by the $50 million special vote to the superannuation account which was appropriated in last year's final supplementaries. Taking this year's main estimates and supplementaries and comparing them with last year's main estimates and supplementaries, I am asking parliament to vote the Department of Finance about $9 million less than a year ago.
While parliament is not called upon to vote the statutory items I should like to refer to them. In the Department of Finance statutory items constitute more than 95 per cent of total expenditures. In the printed record these items add up to almost $1,100 million and show an increase of $154 million over last year. Of this $154 million increase, $128 million was in increased transfer payments to the provincial governments. After the book of estimates was printed the province of Ontario decided to levy and collect its own corporation income tax. This is the principal reason why our transfer payments to the provincial governments will be


$10 million less rather than $128 million more than a year ago. In total, I expect the statutory expenditures relating to the Department of Finance to be not much more than $40 million over last year and this will be wholly due to the higher cost of the public debt.
Hon. members will not be surprised if 1 say that the Department of Finance, which is not a large operating department, is usually able to estimate its administration expenses quite accurately and that it does not provide much place for operating economies. I shall, however, be able to move a small reduction in vote 121 when we reach that item.
Mr. Chairman, I have been asked several times in the house to give a financial statement. I welcome this opportunity of doing so and not least of all because of some of the things that are currently being said outside this house. The Globe and Mail of December 5 contains a news article from which I read the following:
London, Ontario, December 4-Unless the Conservatives make drastic cuts in expenditures the government will end up with a deficit by the end of the fiscal year next March, former finance minister Walter Harris, predicted here today.
We shall see shortly.
The Toronto Telegram of December 5 ascribes to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre a statement made, I believe, in the city of Hamilton the previous night. The article says he accused the government of "hiding the books from parliament until after the next election." I doubt if any of the members of the audience who heard the hon. member make that statement, if he did make it, would be so gullible as to believe it. There will be an opportunity of judging shortly whether that is a responsible or an irresponsible statement.
I would like to make this comment in advance of giving to the house the details of the financial statement. When this government came into office on the 21st day of June the fiscal year was already three months advanced. The programs for the year had largely been undertaken; expenditures and commitments had been entered into. We entered upon our tasks while the government was already in midstream and that fact I think should be borne in mind as we weigh and assess what the government has been able to do.
My predecessor, in presenting the budget for the current fiscal year last March, forecast revenues of $5,170 million; expenditures of $5,018 million and a surplus of $152 million. We have now reasonably complete figures for eight months of the year and thus are able to make revised estimates which

reflect both the changes in economic development and changes in government policies.
On the revenue side of the accounts I am prepared to accept the forecast which was presented to the house last March. At present it seems probable that receipts from income taxes will be somewhat above the forecast and revenues from customs duties and some commodity taxes will be somewhat below the earlier anticipations, but, on balance, I expect that the various increases and decreases will just about cancel each other out, leaving the total revenue figure unchanged at $5,170 million.
On the expenditures side of the accounts my predecessor had forecast a total of $5,018 million. Since then there have been substantial increases in expenditure arising in part out of changing economic developments and in part from new policies which we have recommended and which parliament has approved. For example, we are having to find an additional $25 million for interest and other charges on the public debt as a result of the sharp increase in interest rates which occurred during the spring and summer months. Then I am advised by the management of Canadian National Railways that reduction in the volume of rail traffic and higher costs of operation will mean that we shall have to meet a deficit in the railway's operation of about $28 million.
On the policy side, hon. members will recall that increases in public service salaries and in the defence services pay and allowances have been approved in an amount which will total about $100 million for the 11 months of the fiscal year commencing May 1, including statutory matching payments into the superannuation account. The increase in old age pensions is responsible for most of the increased deficit in the old age security fund of $50 million. Increases in our contributions to old age assistance and to the blind and disabled persons allowances will cost the federal treasury an additional $1 million this year. Increases in veterans benefits will add a further $3 million to this year's expenditures, and the recent agreement with the provinces to eliminate the "threshold" on unemployment assistance will also cost us $3 million in this fiscal year. All these increases add up to $210 million.
Against this large increase in expenditures we have been able to make substantial savings. While the increases in civil service and defence services pay and allowances will cost $100 million the departments have found it possible, by general economies, to absorb part of this increase and, in fact, only $76

In addressing ourselves to the task of eliminating unnecessary expenditure we have been guided by two principles: first that there shall be no reduction in any essential public service and, second, that where items involve construction which means employment, those items are not being reduced. Furthermore, by careful scrutiny and by controlling certain expenditure programs my colleagues have been able to indicate various reductions and savings in estimated expenditure which will add up to almost exactly $40 million. In addition my colleagues have been able to curtail certain loans and advances in the amount of about $6 million.
Finally, I do not propose to adopt the practice of my predecessor to transfer large lump sums of $50 million each into what he called "the reserve against assets" and to reduce the unamortized deficit in the superannuation account. I consider it quite unnecessary to do so.

I have also been asked at different times as to what is the government's financial program. I should now like to indicate the intentions of the government in the matter of financial and fiscal changes which will be submitted to the house in due course for legislative action.
This, as hon. members do not need to be reminded, is not an ordinary or regular session. It is a session called in the fall of the year under circumstances that limited the duration of the session. Its purposes, as the Leader of the Opposition well indicated a few days ago were, first, to vote the approximately 800 items of supply which had not been voted at the time of dissolution and, second, to afford the government an opportunity of laying before parliament for action this fall that constructive program of legislative action which the electorate of Canada had approved on June 10.
One of the undertakings given to the Canadian people in that campaign by that distinguished man who is today the Prime Minister of Canada was that we would reduce taxes. I am not proposing now nor do I intend to propose at any time in this session any increases of any kind in taxation. That made it quite unnecessary to submit to the house anything resembling a budget. The budget for this year was submitted to the house last spring by the then minister of finance. There will be ample opportunity for every member of the house to express whatever opinions he chooses on any of the matters upon which I am now about to indicate the intentions of the government.
May I in passing point out, Mr. Chairman, that it has been quite impossible in the short space of time the government has been in office to take up those matters which the Minister of Finance normally reviews in preparing a budget. There has been no time in which to deal with the wide range of fiscal matters that come to the Minister of Finance apart from those that relate directly to taxation about which I shall shortly have something to say. But I wish to make it abundantly clear that never have I said that there would be that kind of budget presentation which is characteristic of a normal session of parliament. I have said that we would submit to the house such measures as are required to implement the undertakings which we gave to the public in the campaign; and that, Mr. Chairman, is precisely what we shall do.
There are several matters to which reference must be made which require some remedial legislative action. The bill which I hope to introduce will include a change in

the corporate tax structure which will be, I trust, of benefit to certain small corporations.
But I wish, first of all, to deal with a specific matter affecting construction workers. This is a matter which requires an amendment to the Income Tax Act before the end of this calendar year. It is the matter of certain allowances paid to construction workers by their employers to cover expenses of the worker while he is living away from his normal place of residence for a period of time at a construction site. Hon. members will recall that this problem first was brought to public attention by the publication by the Department of National Revenue of a directive entitled "Information Bulletin No. 10" on July 10, 1956. This directive announced that construction workers must thereafter include for tax purposes certain per diem and other allowances received from their employer, whether paid in cash or in the form of free board and lodging. This matter was debated at some length this spring when income tax amendments were under consideration. Some of us then in opposition protested strongly against the effect of this directive, and finally the then minister of finance stated that the rule contained in Bulletin No. 10 would not apply to incomes in 1956 but that the allowance would be taxed commencing in 1957.
For many years it has been the practice for employers in the construction industry to provide board and lodging for workers at remote sites or to pay them an allowance over and above the going wage as reimbursement for expenses of meals and lodging where those were paid for by the worker himself. It is also customary for the construction employer to bear the expense of transporting employees to distant construction sites and bringing them back to their normal place of residence. Throughout the years this has been normal procedure in this industry, and the construction workers did not include in their income for tax purposes the value of these allowances or expenses paid on their behalf by their employer. Then with the issuance of Bulletin No. 10 in 1956 the previous government made it known that these amounts were taxable under the existing law and employers had been under instruction in 1957 to report those allowances as income of their employees.
It is my intention, Mr. Chairman, to restore the practice which prevailed prior to 1957. In order to put this matter beyond doubt I intend to introduce an appropriate amendment to the Income Tax Act effective from January 1, 1957. This amendment, which is necessarily somewhat technical, will appear in detail in the bill. Briefly it will provide that

if the construction site is so distant that the worker cannot reasonably be expected to return daily to his normal place of residence where he maintains a home in which he lives with his wife or some dependent person, then the construction employee will not be required to include in his income for tax purposes the value of the free board and lodging or reasonable allowances paid to him to cover expenses of meals and lodging, or the value of travelling expenses paid by the employer in transporting him to the site and back home again.
The next matter concerns the corporation tax to be paid by certain corporations earning profits in the province of Ontario. In a normal session a bill to give tax relief measures would be the occasion for dealing with a wide variety of miscellaneous technical changes in the income tax structure. This general review of miscellaneous changes in the law will be undertaken in the course of preparation of the budget for the next session. However, I give public notice now of one particular matter which will be the subject of corrective legislation at the next session.
Under the provisions of section 40 of the Income Tax Act, federal corporation income tax is reduced by nine percentage points on profits earned in a "prescribed" province: that is, in a province that does not rent this tax field to the federal government pursuant to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Agreements Act. This tax abatement enables a province to impose its own tax up to this nine per cent level without raising the combined tax above the general federal rate.
In the five-year period prior to 1957 the federal tax abatement was only seven percentage points and Quebec was the only province imposing its own corporate tax of seven per cent. For 1957 Ontario became a prescribed province and profits earned in the province from January 1, 1957 onward accordingly became entitled to a reduction of nine percentage points in their federal tax. Inadvertently, however, the law introduced by the former government in granting this reduction for 1957 gave also to Ontario companies whose fiscal year does not coincide with the calendar year abatement in respect of that portion of their profits earned in 1956. This pattern of reduction was, of course, appropriate and necessary for profits in Quebec since Quebec was taxing profits in 1956. The result of this fault in the federal legislation is, however, that relief is given at the rate of seven percentage points for corporations earning profits in Ontario for a period when no Ontario tax was imposed at all. Obviously this error must be corrected, otherwise about $12 mililon of unintended tax relief would
Supply-Finance
go to a particular group of non-calendar year companies earning profits in the province of Ontario at a time when no provincial tax was imposed upon them.
I have already reminded the committee that this government promised if elected to power to reduce taxes. It is our purpose, sir, scrupulously to fulfil this promise. I do not need to tell hon. members that it is one of the more pleasant duties of the Minister of Finance to come before the house and announce some reduction in the heavy burden of taxes that previous governments have imposed on the people of Canada.
The bill which I shall introduce will include a change in the corporate tax structure which would be particularly important for small corporations. At present the low tax rate of 20 per cent is confined to profits up to $20,000 per annum. In future, from January 1 onward, the low tax rate will extend up to profits of $25,000. Of course, every corporation with profits in excess of this figure will enjoy some benefit from this tax concession but the change will be of greatest significance to relatively small corporations. About 2,000 corporations with profits between $20,000 and $25,000 will have the tax on profits within this range reduced from 47 per cent to 20 per cent. This relief measure will cost the treasury about $12 million on a full year basis and about $1 million in the current fiscal year and I believe it will give a stimulus and incentive to business in small corporations.

I have a word to say on the subject of estate tax. I intend forthwith to place on the order paper a resolution to permit the introduction of a new measure to repeal the Succession Duty Act and to replace it with a new estate tax act. The measure will apply the estate tax principle rather than the inheritance or succession principle. In keeping with the policy of the government it will be another tax reduction measure. It will also greatly simplify the taxation of estates. I shall reserve extended comments until I move the resolution in due course.
For the present I point out that in every tax bracket the tax payable under the new law will be less than under the present Succession Duty Act. All estates will be fully exempted up to a minimum of $50,000. No estate of lower aggregate value will pay any estate tax whatever. In the case of an estate passing to a widow there will be an exemption of $60,000 plus $10,000 for each child under 21 years of age. Thus, if a husband dies leaving a widow and one child under 21 years of age there will be no tax payable unless the value of the estate exceeds $70,000. If he leaves a widow and two children under 21 years of age no estate tax will be payable unless the aggregate value of the estate exceeds $80,000. If he leaves a widow and three children under 21 years of age no estate tax will be payable unless the aggregate value of the estate exceeds $90,000. If he leaves a widow and four children under 21 years of age no estate tax will be payable unless the aggregate value of the estate exceeds $100,000.
The annual loss of revenue to the treasury will be $6 to $8 million. About 40 per cent of this reduction will go to the smallest group of taxable estates, namely those between $50,000 and $75,000. For estates of this size the average reduction is approximately 70 per cent.
It is not intended, sir, to ask the house to advance this bill at the present session beyond first reading. It is desirable that the bill be given first reading and be circulated among hon. members and be available to the public, particularly the members of the legal and accountancy professions. Their views

and suggestions on this major measure will be sought and it will be the intention of the government, with the assistance of suggestions from these sources, to ask parliament to enact the measure at the 1958 session.
May I now summarize the effect of the changes on the balance of ways and means for the present fiscal year? The tax changes I shall be proposing will benefit the car buyer immediately, but because of the time required to put new tax deduction tables into effect, the income tax reductions, although applicable to the full calendar year 1958, may not in all cases be reflected in pay envelopes and salary cheques until February; but this work will be done, I assure the committee, with all possible speed.
While the total tax reductions will add up to $178 million in a full year, the Minister of Finance's cash receipts will be affected by only some $26 million prior to March 31. speechtext: I am going to come to that. Just content yourselves. This, of course, is in very vivid contrast to the statement made last June 25 to the Canadian Press and the British United Press by the minister, before he put in these 17 hours a day every day that there would be a fall budget with tax reductions and pension boosts. He went on to say that he was going to reduce taxes, increase old age pensions and curb government spending in the budget which he was going to bring down. Well, right after that day a pall of silence fell on the usually very talkative and very voluble minister. The press reported that a telephone call by the Prime Minister told him to stop talking and to start working.
