speechtext: I had no telephone call from the Prime Minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Since the session opened I and other members have tried our best to get him to tell us the date of this budget that he said would be presented. He did not say directly. He did not actually deny what the Canadian Press and the British United Press had

Supply-Finance
reported but he left that impression in everyone's mind. He said, of course, that the constitutional practice would be followed. Then we began to suspect there was not going to be a budget so we changed our questioning from when is the budget going to be presented to will there be a budget, and finally after the minister's evasions, we had to turn to the Prime Minister to get an answer. He did answer, as found on page 1710 of Hansard, and told us that there would be no budget this session. He gave a very airy answer saying that he had studied the history of parliament since confederation and had found that in the second sessions of 1873, 1919, 1930 and 1947 no budgets had been presented.
I have checked the four precedents he offered to the house. There is no Hansard for 1873 in the library but there is a scrapbook of accounts of the debates in those days. There was one short session on the railway scandal, the famous Tory railway scandal of 1873. There were no financial proposals made other than the financial proposals made in telegrams from the Tory prime minister at that time to prominent Tories around the country.
In 1919 there was a second session called by Sir Robert Borden and in the speech from the throne only one thing was mentioned, ratification of the Versailles peace treaty which had been signed on June 28. Nobody asked for a budget because no tax measures of any significance were proposed at that session. So there was no precedent there.
Now we roll along to 1930 with a Conservative government again in power. They too pledged a fall session of parliament, and in the throne speech again there was only one subject mentioned, unemployment, a problem which our new Conservative government is certainly having to grapple with. Mr. Bennett declared it was the sole issue of the session. Twenty million dollars was voted for immediate relief and amendments were made to the dumping laws and to the tariff, not for revenue, said Mr. Bennett, but to protect the Canadian workingman. If revenue resulted from these acts the plan would fail because they would not have halted distress selling from other countries. Again no member asked for any budget discussion at that time because obviously neither budgetary nor tax measures were being considered.
I have read those debates with great interest. I was not in the country at the time of the 1930 election. I was a student in Europe. It was very interesting to read and see that that Conservative government, like the present Conservative government,

came to power with a tremendous number of promises, but in fairness to Mr. Bennett
1	must say he ran No. 2 both in number and size of promises to the present Prime Minister. Both, however, made the promise that they would immediately call parliament to carry out their promises. Well, Mr. Bennett made a pretty good fist of that. The election was on July 28 and on September
2	parliament sat. Of course, we heard after June 10 there was going to be an immediate session of parliament but that did not take place until October 14 and today, December 6, we are still waiting for this budget which was promised by the minister last June 25.
We roll along then to 1947. There was no fall session in 1947. The 1948 parliament began in December, 1947, but in that 1947-48 session there was a regular presentation of the budget in the ordinary way. My friend, the Minister of Agriculture, mentioned budget by radio. It is quite true that on November 17 the then minister of finance went on the C.B.C. radio to announce two actions he was taking under two acts of parliament, the Foreign Exchange Control Act and the transitional powers act, in order to stop the drain of our money reserves to the United States, the so-called austerity program.
Our reserves had fallen from over $1,200 million at the beginning of the year to less than $500 million at that time. These two measures, curtailment by quotas of United States imports and an excise tax to discourage the buying of non-essential goods, were announced that night. Parliament met in December and the second order of business was parliamentary approval of these two actions. That is why the minister said then, as Mr. Bennett said in 1930, that there was no budget by radio because these two measures were not designed to increase revenue but rather to restrict the importation of United States goods.
So I say there is no precedent in Canadian parliamentary history for a new session of a new parliament not having a budget. It is especially significant at this time because never before in Canadian history was a party elected on a platform of so many expensive promises, and so many high tax cuts, promises and policies that were obviously going to have a very profound effect on the balance of ways and means. As far as other members of the House of Commons are concerned, as far as the people of the nation are concerned, the only way they will learn the impact of the new proposals made, the many new proposals we are waiting for if their promises are going to be implemented, and also the tax cuts-not the small ones mentioned tonight but the ones I am going to mention which

were promised in the election-is for the people to be given an accounting and a balance sheet. In other words, they want the usual budget debate which characterizes every formal session of parliament.
What does a budget debate entail? First of all, it does entail a fair measure of warning. I looked back in Hansard and over the last 20 years there was a warning of anywhere from five days to two weeks of the actual date on which the budget was going to be produced. Then, there was a white paper produced the day before the budget. Last year it was a document of 90 pages containing many figures. In this way every member would know exactly the up to date figures on the economic state of the nation on gross national product, on trade, on the balance of payments and on the revenues from the various tax fields. We would have that before us when we listened to the minister and before we made our own speeches.
In addition, there was the courtesy extended that the hon. member for Greenwood mentioned earlier, that, as the minister began his speech, and it was generally a long speech, he sent a copy of his proposals across to the leaders of the various groups so that they could read all the figures there and be ready when he concluded his remarks to make some statements on them. Tonight we have had no such information. I understand the press gallery also has had no information. We jot down these figures as best we can as the minister speaks, and will have to wait now until these tables appear in Hansard in the morning before we really understand.
Finally, the minister stood up in his place at eight o'clock on the appointed night, with the Speaker in the chair, and moved a motion for ways and means. By our rule book he is given unlimited time, as he should have, in proposing such an essential statement for the people of this country, and the first speaker replying to him is given the same privilege. This is the constitutional practice, and is the practice which has been followed since confederation. Our new Minister of Finance, however, beat a new trail. He chose to use item 1 of his estimates to make this budget statement. I looked back over the last 12 presentations of finance estimates, which cover the period the hon. member has been in the house, and in 11 out of those 12 years there was no statement whatever made on item 1. In one year the minister of finance, in response to a request from the Social Credit party, gave a short two page statement on fiscal and monetary policy. It is quite true that other ministers in other departments sometimes choose to make a fairly extended statement
Supply-Finance
on item 1 outlining the work of their department during the previous year. I, myself, when I was Minister of Fisheries followed that course.
The reason ministers of finance never have followed such a course is that traditionally they have had a very much better opportunity in the budget debate to put before parliament the whole story of the balance sheet of Canada. This, however, has been denied us by the present procedure. Let us just compare that traditional procedure with what has happened today; this queer way of doing business as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar rightly calls it. First of all, instead of five days or two weeks warning we had really no warning at all. Yesterday morning, according to Hansard, the Minister of Finance assured this house that the finance estimates would not come before parliament today. At ten o'clock last night, after prodding by the house leader of the official opposition, it was brought out that at eight o'clock tonight, despite the assertions of the Minister of Finance, we would be into finance tonight. We had, therefore, no warning.
Secondly, we have no basic material. There is no white paper produced. There was no white paper produced either by the Minister of National Defence when we started on his estimates a day or two ago, the biggest block of estimates presented to this house. Another weakness at the present time with this procedure is the failure of the minister to make a statement in the house which, in my time, Mr. Ilsley, Mr. Abbott and Mr. Harris have made, inviting members of the opposition to make full use so far as finding factual information is concerned, of the very able officers of the Department of Finance. Having spent four years as assistant to the minister of finance, I have formed a very high opinion of their services. I recall that the hon. member for Greenwood, when he was financial critic, took great advantage of that offer and that staff. These civil servants, after all, are not solely serving the government. We would not expect them to reveal policy to us in the opposition, but it would be very helpful if we could have access to them for factual information.
You might say, why did 1 not approach them anyhow, without invitation? We have heard statements from the Minister of Public Works and others recently about the very high value they place on the civil servants of Canada. These statements are certainly well deserved. However, we also heard rumblings from the patronage-hungry Tories rebuking the Minister of Public Works for saying there was going to be no patronage. The hon. member for Victoria returned to

Supply-Finance
British Columbia after a caucus meeting of Conservative members last summer and spoke at a meeting of the Oak Bay Progressive Conservative association on September 17. I shall take this report from the Victoria Colonist because it is the Tory paper. It reads:
Civil Service "Brass" All Grits, Tories find.
The heat is on the top brass of the civil service in Ottawa, A. DeB McPhillips, Victoria MP, told the Oak Bay Progressive Conservative Association last night.
The government now is in the process of breaking down the all-Grit top echelon of the civil service, he said.
"All the top civil servants and the deputy ministers are Grits," he told the meeting.
"Don't be impatient at government action," he said. "After the next election when we have a more secure mandate, more stern action will be taken."
I certainly was not going to embarrass any of the top echelon in the finance department by going to them and asking for factual information, and having them fired.

speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
I would certainly appreciate one of the ministers repudiating the statement which was made after the Tory caucus by the hon. member for Victoria.
Then, even in the ways and means committee, if we finally got there, there would be 48 hours notice given on each of these money resolutions. Instead this new minister chose this unique way of using item 1 of his estimates to make this extraordinarily important statement on finance. He knew that the 30-minute rule on debate applied, and that is why we drew it to his attention and the attention of the nation. He chose a field in which he, himself, would be limited in the account which he gave to the nation. It is for that reason we have had no statement from him on trade, balance of payments gross national production, or any of the many economic aspects which are usually and properly reviewed in such a budget speech.
Of course, this queer way of doing business could have been avoided if he had followed, as he said he would, the constitutional practice of the Canadian parliament; if he had gone ahead with his solemn promise of last summer that there would be a budget; even if he had changed his mind-there is nothing wrong about changing your mind, if he had told us. Today the minister who sits behind him, the Minister of Labour, got up and frankly admitted he had made a mistake. We accepted that without any criticism. We all make mistakes, that is everybody except the Minister of Finance. He would not tell the house he had changed his mind and did not intend to have a budget; he let that pass to the Prime Minister to make such an announcement.
With that explanation of this unusual course, I want now to start touching on some of the remarks the minister just made in this abbreviated budget discussion. I start out by saying that no minister of finance in Canadian history has been quite so lucky as this minister. He has been lucky in the fact that he is blessed with extraordinary talents; he has told us so himself. He is a hard worker; he has told us so himself, and also unlike most previous ministers of finance he started with a $500 million surplus in the kitty. Most new ministers of finance, of course, come in when the exchequer is empty. This minister had a start of $500 million.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Since when? Where did that come from?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
I shall be very happy to tell you where it came from. Last session the minister of finance did present his estimates of revenues, and he estimated that the surplus was going to be $282 million. But never once did any Tory in this house accept that. The minister himself, at page 2556 of Hansard of last session, said that by his calculations the surplus was going to be $518 million. We corrected that assertion quite often, but hon. members of the Tory party would not listen to us.
Then, they went out during the last election campaign and announced across the country, "You are overtaxed by $500 million." Here is just a sample. The hon. member for Huron probably recognizes these advertisements from the Seaforth Expositor.-"500 million surplus." The hon. member for Hamilton South will perhaps recognize this full page advertisement, "Surplus $500 million; Vote for Bob McDonald." Here is another one mentioning the $500 million surplus that the Liberals had taxed from the people. Night after night the Prime Minister made these great declarations that every Canadian family-there are over four million of them- is overtaxed by $120 and that is $500 million a year.
It is for that reason I say the minister was a lucky man to start off with this great $500 million surplus. He has another favourite figure-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
He
is never wrong.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Oh, he is never wrong, he said that himself. Another great figure we have seen across the nation in relation to these estimates-and we have books of these promises-was that in relation to essential services. He was going to trim an amount of $500 million from the estimates without

affecting essential services. Well, once again he has adopted a queer way of doing business. In tabling the main estimates prepared by the former government at the beginning of the session he said he was tabling them but some of the items he did not stand behind. He was going to remove some and reduce some but did not specify and the Leader of the Opposition and others over here said "Well, give us a list of the items you do not stand behind." But he has refused to do that up to now. So, as each department has come along, we have asked "What part of the $500 million of waste and extravagance have you found in your department?" Well, my hon. friend the Minister of Transport, who is a man who will face up to things said last September he had found no waste or extravagance in his well-run department. The Secretary of State said the same thing-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: I never did.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: And the minister of mines-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: On a point of order, I said no such thing. If the hon. member will read Hansard he will find out exactly what I did say.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: I should of course permit the hon. lady to have the last word but if she will read Hansard she will find that her estimates were not reduced by $1-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: And I explained that too.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: That is the whole point of this argument; it is not explanations but reductions that the people were led to expect. The minister of mines said the same thing and it was the same in the case of the ministers of veterans affairs and defence and external affairs. I do not know whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce was asked that same question this morning-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
And the Solicitor
General.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Yes, and then today we have at last come to item 1 of the Department of Finance, the second largest department with items totalling almost $1,200 million. A lot of that is statutory, but you would think that probably in his own department that is where he would find a great part of this $500 million of waste and extravagance of which so far we have seen no evidence. He did mention a small saving which he will be able to make on item 121 but he again paid a. sterling tribute to the economy and efficiency with which his department had been run so we cannot expect very much there.
Supply-Finance
Now I turn to this matter of tax cuts. I do not want to break the rules of this house by going overtime-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: First time you did not want to break them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: No, no, but that was the promise made. The Prime Minister again and again said there would be a great tax reduction; $120 per family or $500 million all told. The excise tax would be removed by them. I do not need to quote the Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Go ahead.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: It is worth quoting.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Well this figure of $500 million is so well known, and he said that these were solemn obligations which would be effectuated so we naturally expected in this debate tax cuts totalling $500 million. We expected them to be retroactive. On platform after platform he said $10 a month excess tax was being taken out of every family in Canada by the Liberal government. Well now by their failure to correct this situation after almost six months in office they have put a load of $60 extra taxation on every one of these poor families.
I say that tonight the minister groaned and produced a very small mouse in the way of income tax reductions. The 1949 Tory platform and the proposals of their financial critic, the member for Greenwood, were to raise the basic exemption from $1000 to $1,250 and from $2,000 to $2,500 for married men which would cost $140 million a year. Well the voters did not go for that so in 1953 they raised the ante and there was the Prime Minister with the Conservative platform promising that if they were elected the basic exemption would immediately be raised for the single man from $1,000 to $1,500 and for the married man $2,000 to $3,000 at a cost of $300 million a year. We do not hear anything of that tonight.
Now according to my figures when I was parliamentary assistant that would be equivalent to a cost of $300 million for the latter proposal and $140 million for the former proposal, an amount which the hon. member for Greenwood at that time characterized as a very small amount. Why then, if it is such a small amount, is it not included tonight. It is a pity it was not included for it would be a real help to the men on low incomes. A man earning less than $3,000 of course would be totally exempt from tax if these solemn promises had been honoured.
There were of course other promises made. The sales tax was one of them. The Tory

Supply-Finance
whip in his ad. promised this in the Seaforth News which I guess is published in his riding.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: By my opposition.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
But said by you. Here are some tax items in his ad.; "under a Conservative government the income tax for a married man would be nothing on $3,000 after election". Then he goes on to mention prepaid health insurance, floor prices on farm products and then removal of all sales tax and "anyone spending $300 on clothing, shoes and so on now pays $30 and after the election"-or after he is elected-"will pay nothing".
Well we did not hear of any removal of the sales tax tonight. During the election the Prime Minister promised at Windsor to reduce the excise tax on cars, and at Oshawa to abolish the tax. Well, again, there is an awful difference between abolishing a tax and the 2J per cent reduction in the tax which is now proposed.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: On a point of order. The Prime Minister stated here that he did not make any such suggestion and the hon. member must accept that statement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Oh no.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: The Prime Minister, according to press accounts said, as the hon. member will note if he actually consults Hansard, that he was going to remove the exise tax completely as it was a horse and buggy tax. Then there is my good friend over there the Minister of Transport on the corporation tax-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The Prime Minister said just a few days ago that he had never said he would remove that tax completely and now the hon. member for Coast-Capilano should not try to put words into his mouth.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that I read an actual clipping from the two Tory papers, the Toronto Telegram and the Ottawa Journal and the Ottawa Citizen, the next day which said that he had promised to abolish this tax. I said and would say that the time to deny that was then, and not six months later.
Now my hon. friend the Minister of Transport over there said he wanted a sliding scale with respect to the corporation tax. Not just a little lift of from $20,000 or $25,000 but a real sliding scale, the whole way up to give real savings, with, the reductions in the corporation taxes, to be at least one-third. He smiles now and I think he still hopes one day this solemn promise may be effectuated. Well, we have not got $500

million nor the reductions tonight as was promised last summer, and solemnly promised.
Then in the figures given in his speech tonight by the minister-and this is one of the disadvantages of not having budget papers in the ordinary way-I think he said that in a full year the tax cuts might amount to $178 million; but would amount to less than $40 million for the present year.
We have heard quite a bit about inflation this session but he does not mention that at all in his budget speech. This is another convenience he has found in choosing supply so he would have to shorten his speech so that such things as inflation and the balance of ways and means could not be covered by him. Inflation has been a very serious problem and the previous government two years ago took brave but unpopular and misunderstood actions-misunderstood mainly because of the attempts of the conservatives to mislead the public about the dangers of inflation and what was being done by the then government. Now the Minister of Finance says we have checked inflation and he went all the way down to Hollywood, Florida which I guess is a place which combines both the attractions of Florida and California, to make a speech to the United States investors apparently to tell them that he was not as mad at them as some of his speeches made in Canada might lead them to believe and on page 11 of his speech to American investors he says this:
In recent years the Canadian economy, like that of the United States, has been pursued by the ever-increasing threat of inflation. I confidently say to you that inflation has been checked.
I would say that if it has been checked it was checked through brave action taken by Mr. Harris and the governor of the Bank of Canada over the last two years. I said, "If it has been checked"; because I am going to quote a little better financial authority than the hard-working, ever modest Minister of Finance. I have just finished reading the annual report of the Bank of Montreal, Canada's leading bank. In the president's statement this is what he has to say:
Canada, with its network of close economic and other international ties, would be hiding its head in the sand to assume that the fight against inflation had been won.
Take your choice, the president of the Bank of Montreal speaking to Canadians, or the Minister of Finance speaking to Americans in Florida. But you do not quite have to take your choice because this morning the attention of the house was drawn to the fact that the money rate is going back up. Treasury rates are climbing and of course

the Bank of Canada rate climbs as a consequence. It was very interesting, of course, to note that when the treasury rate was falling the Minister of Finance-nice modest little fellow that he is-gathered all the credit to himself. As reported at page 1564 of Hansard, when he announced a reduction in the bank rates he had this to say:
The government will certainly claim the credit that is its due for a great many things it has done to seek to ease money, credit and interest rates, and is very gratified that its efforts in this regard have borne fruit.
That is when the interest rate goes down. But when the interest rate goes up, like Pontius Pilate he washes his hands of the affair and has nothing to do with it. Again he is such a modest little fellow.
Now I get along to the balance of ways and means. The fact that we have not a white paper makes it exceedingly difficult for any member of the opposition accurately to calculate what is the present balance between revenues and expenditures in this country. We know that some great expenditures have been promised. The Financial Post estimates that the new expenditures already effectuated to date have cost this country another $300 million. I, in my own modest way, have tried to make some calculations of what all the promises of the Tory party would total, and I find that the ones mentioned so far would add about $1,200 million to the annual budget and I am not including some projects. I see my friend the Minister of Public Works smiling at me.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: He is laughing, not smiling.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
After he left Vancouver as a minister of the new government he said that the first task of this government was going to be to rebuild the Canadian merchant marine. That is going to cost $250 million at the very minimum. While he promised that, our friend over here the Minister of Transport is busy stripping off the last eight ships of the Canadian merchant navy and putting them under a foreign flag. That is why I did not include that cost in the $1,200 million of my estimate. I am a little bit confused as to which of these ministers is going to have his way in the end.
Then, of course, we have no mention of the dominion-provincial tax agreements. If there is going to be any more money for the ten provinces before the end of the fiscal year, it must be provided now by the minister. Premier Frost is a modest fellow. All he wants now is $100 million a year extra, which means $200 million extra for the other provinces, an extra total of $300 million. Premier Bennett of British Columbia is not a
Supply-Finance
modest man; he is like the Minister of Finance. He wants another $960 million to be given to the provinces.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: I am sorry to advise the hon. member that his time has expired.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is all very enjoyable. We should be glad to have some more.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: The house leader knows the rules limiting speeches to thirty minutes. But a member can speak as often as he likes on this item No. 1. I shall have therefore more to say on the next time around but unlike the Minister of Finance I will observe the rules at the present time and sit down.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my first word is this. There are a large number of new members in the House of Commons who are not familiar with the procedures of parliament as they have been developed over the years. Consequently I can understand that many of them think that this way of introducing tax reductions and discussing what is in effect a small budget is the usual and traditional way of doing something which is of the utmost importance to the people of Canada and by tradition one of the most important things that parliament does during the session.
This is a session of parliament; at least I understood it was. It was opened by Her Majesty the Queen as a session,-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Very formally.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Very formally indeed, as my hon. friend reminds me. Consequently in this session of parliament we had certainly expected that the government would come before us and present the country's balance sheet, the country's budget. I say that failure to do this is something that should be regarded by this house and indeed by the country with utmost seriousness for it is something that has never happened before. Certainly we in this house did not expect that this would be undertaken by a government headed by the Prime Minister. No one in the last parliament talked more often or at greater length or talked more during the election period or at greater length about the supremacy of parliament and the necessity to restore the rights of parliament than did the present Prime Minister of Canada. Yet today we see set aside one of the parliamentary methods of reviewing the work of the government and particularly its financial affairs and the government refusing to bring in a proper balance sheet.

Supply-Finance
Tonight we had nothing about the productivity of Canada. We have had no word as to what the gross national product is likely to be. We have some word of what the government expects its receipts and expenditures may be for the year. We are told that there will be a surplus of some $80 million. But when you come to look at that surplus of $80 million, how does the hon. member obtain it? He obtains it by transferring two items of $50 million. Consequently the idea that there will be a surplus of $80 million is altogether wrong.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
It
is a bookkeeping trick.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Yes; it is a bookkeeping trick. It is merely a bookkeeping transfer. That is all it is.
Secondly, we have heard a great deal about the expected surplus outlined by the former minister of finance. I believe that the former minister of finance, when he put before the house the suggestion that he might have a very substantial surplus, believed in his heart that that surplus would not materialize by March 31, 1958. Why? Because he expected during the current year that the federal treasury would have to do something for the health plan that had been adopted in March by this parliament. In the estimates placed before this house tonight by the Minister of Finance no mention has been made of the possibility of the federal government having to contribute to any of the six provinces that have come to agreement with this government and this parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: They have not signed them yet.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Yet the Prime Minister has told us, when he has been twitted, that this health plan or this hospitalization plan will come into effect sooner than you think. How soon?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: And it will.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
The minister says it will. Very well. Why did not the Minister of Finance, if it is coming in soon, tell us what it is going to cost, and how much of the $80 million will be allocated to the provinces during the next few months because there are provinces with their health plans in operation and ready and anxious to sign and properly entitled to receive the grants under the legislation that we passed in this house last March. Then again, he has told us nothing about what he is going to do for agriculture.
We are going to have an agricultural measure in this house that we hope at least will do something for the farmers of this

country. We are hoping that some provision will be made for deficiency payments. We are hoping that some means will be found to give the farmers something of parity for their products. This legislation is supposed to be brought in. What is it going to cost? The Minister of Finance has had nothing to say about the cost of these worth-while additional expenditures that this parliament will be called upon to make, I hope, within the next few months. There was no mention of agriculture, no mention of a health plan and no mention of the gross national product and what we may expect during the next few months of this current financial year in that regard.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: He is on the skids.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
True, the statement the
minister made tonight does envisage some tax reductions which will be welcome. The reduction of the excise tax from 10 per cent to 74 per cent will be welcomed by the automobile industry and more particularly by the dealers if they are relieved of the loss that they might otherwise have sustained. The people of Canada will welcome this measure if the automobile industry passes on this saving to the people. But even that is not what was expected. We have been told that this tax is a pernicious tax and that it would be wiped out.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: It was described as a horse and buggy tax.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: We were told that it would be cut down to five per cent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD

speechtext: There was a leak.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: It was generally stated. My hon. friends criticized that tax in toto.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Horse and buggy tax.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Yes, a horse and buggy tax.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: We agree that it is.

speechtext: The government promised it would be wiped out.

speechtext:
Members of the government electioneered about the tax and criticized it in toto. They promised if they were elected that it would be reduced more drastically than it was tonight. Why was it not reduced

to a greater extent? Perhaps they did not want the people to give any credence to the leak that was generally supposed to have occurred during the past week or ten days.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: My hon. friends can groan as they like but they are going to groan a lot more in the next few years.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: You are groaning now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: And there will be weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth, too.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: We have had tonight an excuse for a budget.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: A pretty good excuse.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: The Minister of National Health and Welfare laughs-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: -but let him read his Canadian history and his British history and he will find that what has been done tonight is unprecedented in two particulars. The first is that the government has refused to bring down a financial statement, a budget, into this house. The second is that this has been introduced in the house without a motion in committee of ways and means so there can be no real debate on the proposals of the minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: What is going on now?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: This is not a proper debate. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano and I cannot move an amendment. We are only discussing the first item of the estimates.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: You would not debate it even if you could.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
You do not
vote for your amendments.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Oh yes we
do.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext: My hon. friend mentioned the fact that the Prime Minister, last Monday, December 2, attempted to justify this kind of caricature of parliament, as he described something that occurred in the house in June, 1956, by saying that this had been done before. I want to tell you that it has never been done before. My hon. friend quoted the precedents. What were those precedents? Well, he described them to us. The first occurred in the session of 1873. What length of time did the house meet in 1873?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
That was a long time ago.
Supply-Finance

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRING FLAX AND RYE UNDER JURISDICTION OF BOARD
speechtext:
Eleven days. As my hon.
friend already said that was the session of the infamous Pacific scandal but what he did not mention-and perhaps my hon. friend forgot to mention it-was that there were no tax changes in those eleven days so there was no need for a budget in that session.
The next example was that of 1919, a slightly longer session. Again the Prime Minister neglected to inform us last Monday that there were no changes in taxation during that short session which lasted less than a month as I recall it. I would not want to say definitely how long it lasted because my memory may be at fault in that particular.
The session of 1930 which was cited as another example lasted twelve days and was looked upon as an emergency session. Unemployment was rampant, farm prices had fallen and even some of our great banks and insurance companies were in a very uncertain position, so uncertain a position my hon. friends may remember that the government of that day passed two orders in council in 1930 or 1931 authorizing the banks and insurance companies to publish balance sheets showing their assets valued not at the end of the year when those orders in council were passed but prior to the depression.
The Hon. Mr. Power who is now in the Senate and the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley who is now one of our respected judges told this story in the House of Commons two or three years later and you will find it in the records. I have in my files the two orders in council that were passed by the Conservative government at that time covering up the situation that threatened our financial institutions. The emergency session of 1930 lasted twelve days. This, we are told, is a full session of parliament and it was opened, as I said, by Her Majesty the Queen to do the business of the country.

Mr. Chairman, in the few minutes that I have before ten o'clock I should like to make a few general remarks about the most unusual exhibition that we have seen here tonight. I think the method which was taken by the Minister of Finance to announce his tax changes was nothing short of sleight-of-hand and a most unusual method, a method that will make history of a very sorry kind. I say that because unquestionably governments in the future will point to this as a precedent, will attempt to use a similar method and, as the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar has said, perhaps try to go farther and create financial chaos in the country.
I was hoping that the Minister of Finance would realize how important it is for him and his colleagues to observe meticulously the rules of parliament and to see to it that this parliament is supreme. The representatives of the people gathered in this parliament are supreme over the executive. I heard the Minister of Finance three years ago away off in East Africa in the parliament house of Nairobi give a learned discourse on the manner in which the executive branch of government was arrogating unto itself the powers of the legislative branch of government. For quite some time he inveighed against the practice and convinced a lot of people there that the Canadian parliament, in common with many other parliaments in the commonwealth, was perhaps giving over to the executive branch powers that really belong to the legislative branch of government, parliament.
I can see from his performance tonight that he did not convince himself then that his arguments were sound because he has certainly turned his back on what he said that day and has, as I said, followed a most unusual course in bringing in this budget. I think the method he used tonight can best be likened perhaps to a farmer transporting a load of hay out of a prison yard and

Supply-Finance
secreting a criminal under the hay in order to get him out of jail. There is no other likeness.
Here is a method that I deplore. I think the government should be straightforward. It had every reason to be straightforward, and I cannot for the life of me understand why the minister did not go straight ahead with the declaration he made shortly after he came into office that he would present a budget. I realize that the Prime Minister was said to have taken a different view at the time and whether the Prime Minister told the Minister of Finance that he was not to bring in a budget or what nobody will know. I am not going to accuse him of interfering with the Minister of Finance in any way but I will say that once the Minister of Finance said he was going to present a budget at this session I think he should have carried it through. If he felt he was out of harmony with his leader he should have resigned and let some other person assume the post and take a course that would have been more in keeping with the wishes of the Prime Minister.
Certainly this method did not represent the views of the Minister of Finance at that time. Something happened to change his mind. I do not know what it was and I suppose we shall never know. Why no budget? There should have been a budget presented and I have said so on every occasion. I agree with those who have already spoken. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano presented, I thought, a very reasoned argument for having a budget. Certainly if at any time in Canadian history it was necessary for members of parliament to have a white paper, this is it. In all my experience of nearly 23 years in legislative chambers, this is the year when we most needed to have all the facts and figures concerning the economic affairs of the country. Certainly we should have had a balance sheet before us several days ago, even if it were necessary to work the hard-working minister 20 or 30 hours a day.
I sympathize with him in his difficulty in trying to carry the heavy duties of an office with which he was not familiar, and having had no executive experience in government it certainly must have been a terrible job for him to get accustomed to things. I appreciate that fact, but if he had said that he would produce to the very best of his ability all the facts and figures that are available and have them printed in a white paper, which would not have been a terrific job, then we could have had something before us to follow.

I should have liked to have a copy of his speech that he gave tonight. Other ministers have paid us that courtesy. Just after the budget speech was under way they have always had copies sent to us so that we could mark them and follow very carefully as they went along. That did help us considerably. I judge from what is printed here that he considered the Liberals to be the high tax party. I do not know about that. It could be a very serious question that could be debated. There has not been a single word said about the sales tax.
Of course, mind you, it might have been that if they had brought in changes in the sales tax they would have had to bring in a budget. I do not know for certain whether or not that is true. In any event, that may have been another reason, but the fact remains that the government did not come to grips with this very important matter of taxation that does push up prices and cause inflation. I have not yet got at the reason, perhaps, for the failure to produce a budget. I believe we are reasonable people and would reasonably meet any request of that kind to facilitate the business of this country in what is supposed to be a special session.
There is no excuse for the government not having asked us; not one. It is just one more reason why I say that the biggest complaint against the government today is this flouting of parliament. This is the very thing upon which they went to the country; the very thing they claimed to the Canadian people they would have to restore. Moses coming to lead the children of Israel out of bondage; that is what they were going to do. I have not seen any evidence of it. Parliament has not been recognized during this session as they promised it would be recognized. What took place tonight is just one further example of the way parliament is being treated. I say that that is not the way to gain the confidence of the people of this country, not at all. It is certainly the best way to lead the people to demand that a change be made for the better. The consideration of the financial statement of the year, familiarly known as "the budget", is made when the finance minister has completed his estimates of the probable income and expenditure for the year and usually after some progress has been made in voting the main estimates laid on the table. It is usual to make the budget speech on the motion for the house to go into committee of ways and means; but finance ministers have at times found it convenient to make it on the motion for committee of supply.
I cite that to show that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was quite wrong in what he had to say tonight. If a further authority is required on the subject, it is set out in May. I am quoting from May's 15th edition, pages 760 and 764. The following is to be found at page 760:
Matters which are covered by the term "charges upon the people" may be briefly summarized as (1) the imposition of taxation, including the increase in rate, or extension in incidence, of existing taxation, (2) the repeal or reduction of existing alleviations of taxation such as exemptions or drawbacks, (3) the delegation of taxing powers within the United Kingdom, (4) the granting of borrowing powers and (5) provision for the payment into the exchequer of receipts which do not arise from taxation.

Provisions for the alleviation of taxation-

Provisions for the alleviation of taxation are not subject to the rules of financial procedure. The repeal or reduction of a tax, for instance, by the Finance Bill, is sometimes preceded by a specific ways and means resolution. But this procedure is neither necessary nor usual. Now, Mr. Speaker, the point is that prior to 1880 there was an instance in the Canadian House of Commons of an action such as the one taken by the minister tonight and it is on that basis that Beauchesne put citation 495 in his third edition but, if you look back to the sources of Beauchesne's citation 495, which is page 429 of Bourinot, you will find that it has not happened since 1880.
May I also draw to the attention of the Minister of Finance other citations-I will not take up the time of the house to read them but I will give him the page numbers -418, 428 and 438 of Bourinot, which make it clear that all propositions-not just increases in taxation-relating to the tariff and taxation of the country must be considered in committee of ways and means. At one of the pages I have given Bourinot says that changes in taxation, whether increases, amendments, reductions or abolitions, must be dealt with in committee of ways and means.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that my leader was absolutely correct in what he said as to the impropriety of this way of proceeding in terms of the Canadian practice and that according to Canadian practice and according to our rules there is no question but that these income tax changes have got to be dealt with in the committee of ways and means.
It is also my view-

How long did the
Minister of Finance speak?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I suggest he is within his rights and should not be interfered with in making his point of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Well, I will conclude very briefly with what I have to say. It is my view that the changes we made in our standing orders in 1955, when we separated the rules respecting ways and means from those respecting supply, involved the decision that from then on there was to be only one eight-day debate on the motion to go into committee of ways and means, but there was to be that one debate. Prior to the change in that rule it was possible in one session to have several debates on the motion to go into committee of ways and means and it was agreed in the committee on procedure that maybe that was unnecessary. The change we made in 1955 provided for incidental occasions on which we can go into committee of ways and means without question put, but for the one main budget debate of the session there must be the motion, which is subject to one amendment and one subamendment, and the debate must not exceed eight days.
Those were the new rules.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There may be some argument about the interpretation of that rule, Mr. Speaker, for the reason that it has never been tested since it was changed in 1955. I did not think the party across the way would test it. But though there could be a discussion about the requirement that there should be a debate with the Speaker in the chair before we go into committee of ways and means on proposals such as those made tonight, there is no question but that any taxation changes have to be made in committee of ways and means. I consider that our discussion on these taxation measures, taking place in committee of supply, is really out of order, for resolutions will have to be moved in committee of ways and means and it is therefore possible that all the speeches which have been made tonight may be made all over again and nobody could complain.
I submit that when the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary assistant, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), start looking to the authorities, they should look to authorities that are valid with respect to our Canadian practices.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat my question. Is the Minister of Finance giving notice of resolutions to be moved in committee of ways and means?

1.	How many of the patrol boats in the protection service of the Department of Fisheries are used mainly to enforce the 12-mile fishing limit?
2.	What was the date of the first order in council establishing the 12-mile limit for Canadian trawlers?
Answer by: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of
Fisheries):
1.	No patrol boat is occupied full time in such enforcement. The work is mainly carried on by C.G.S. Cygnus. Assistance is given by six of the department's larger patrol boats.
2.	April 6, 1915.

ELECTRICITY COST, NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
1.	What is the cost of electricity generated from thermal sources to industrial users in Nova Scotia?
2.	What will be the cost to same users as a result of subvention on coal for power purposes?
Questions
Answer by: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Secretary of State):
1.	This information is not available in the dominion bureau of statistics. A separate breakdown for industrial users is not compiled.
2.	The subvention to be paid on coal for power purposes is part of agreements under negotiation with the authorities in the maritime provinces. Until the agreements are finally concluded, it is not possible to state any figures on the consequent reductions in the cost of power.
